| **Permission-Rail Feed Loss (F4b)**           | Feed to the permission rail's hold-up store opened during the longest stop the enforcer can admit on an inspected floor, from its `{python} RackEndVerification.ceiling_insp_str` ceiling | Permission path, drive logic, and brake coils run on the store; powered drive energy remains separately available                                                                                   | Feed-loss flag on the permission rail                                                                                                                           | Complete the resident stop; set every spring brake at standstill                        | Stop completes and every brake sets before the rail reaches dropout (`{python} RackEndVerification.flag_to_set_str` of the `{python} RackEndVerification.rail_holdup_str` hold-up); any reset is `FAIL`                                                      |
| **Actuator Jam & Mechanical Stall**           | Wheel bearing seizure or dragging brake, injected via wheel clamp or dynamometer                                                                                                          | Locked rotor; one wheel blocked yaws the base; rapid stator winding heating ($I^2 R$)                                                                                                               | Motor phase overcurrent & Hall-effect velocity stall monitor, within its detection bound                                                                        | De-energize the power stage; engage the spring-applied brake                            | Winding temperature remains below the chosen operating ceiling in @sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles; base stays inside the `{python} RackEndVerification.side_clearance_str` side clearance                                                                      |
| **Proposer Injection: Instruction or Visual** | Adversarial instruction text on the task channel, or a printed patch, label, or sign placed in the intent model's camera view                                                             | Well-formed proposals that pursue the attacker's goal; every field, timestamp, and lease is valid                                                                                                   | No check on the proposal's meaning; speed, force, swept-volume occupancy, stopping-reserve, and freshness checks on every tick                                  | Clamp or refuse the proposal like any other; wrong actions inside the envelope continue | Every proposal that breaches a monitored limit is clamped or refused within the `{python} RackEndVerification.enforcer_deadline_str` enforcer deadline; wrong actions inside the envelope are recorded as coverage deficits, never as passes                 |
| **Authority Transfer (A1): Duplicate Writer** | Second bus master writes a base-drive channel (duplicate EtherCAT identifier or DMA write) while policy and remote assistant both command                                                 | Two writers on one channel; the delivered command is no longer the admitted one                                                                                                                     | Bus or DMA write permissions; per-tick authority log                                                                                                            | Reject the foreign write; the enforcer path remains the only writer                     | Write rejected; every authority-log entry in the window shows one writer                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Authority Transfer (A2): Tier Bypass**      | Policy proposal injected while `MAN` is active; remote-assistant command that opposes the enforcer's admitted limit                                                                       | A lower tier displaces an active higher tier, or an assistant command skips the permission check                                                                                                    | Arbiter tier check; permission check applied to every source                                                                                                    | Ignore the policy proposal; clamp or refuse the assistant command like any proposal     | Arbiter ignores the proposal; the permission check still runs on the assistant's command                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Authority Transfer (A3): Handover Timeout** | Assistant input frozen during `PEND`; acknowledgment frames dropped, at the moving-takeover candidate and aisle speeds                                                                    | The machine waits on a handover that no one completes                                                                                                                                               | Handover deadline timer in the arbiter                                                                                                                          | Reject an infeasible moving handover; start the validated fallback                      | Infeasible moving handover rejected; local stop dispatched by the qualified current-clearance deadline of @sec-intervention-authority-transitions, without awaiting acknowledgment                                                                           |
| **Authority Transfer (A4): Authentication**   | Replayed captured `veto_path`, `manual_drive`, or `accept_item` packet; packet carrying a bad tag                                                                                         | An unauthenticated source gains authority                                                                                                                                                           | Tag and freshness check on every assistant and coworker command                                                                                                 | Reject the packet; rate-limit ingress while preserving valid authority                  | Invalid packet rejected; still-valid authority preserved; rejection recorded; enforcement deadlines met under ingress load                                                                                                                                   |

: **Representative hardware and cyber-physical fault classes**: The rack-end faults F1–F4 and the four authority fault cases (A1–A4) that @sec-intervention-authority-log hands over, each mapped to its injection point, detector, response, and observable pass criterion on the warehouse mobile manipulator, plus one forward-derived mechanical fault and one attack on the learned proposer. {#tbl-15-fault-classification tbl-colwidths="[16,18,18,16,16,16]"}

### Transduction-layer cyber-physical attacks {#sec-verification-transduction-attacks}

The optical, acoustic, and contact disturbances introduced with the operating envelope also become **transduction-layer cyber-physical attacks**\index{Cyber-physical security!transduction attacks}\index{Sensor spoofing!physical injection}\index{Cybersecurity engineering!ISO/SAE 21434} when an adversary induces them. Their verification consequence is the same: a sensor can deliver a well-formed packet whose physical claim is false. Packet integrity therefore cannot serve as the oracle for perception validity.

For an optical disturbance, the test must specify the illumination and approach conditions that challenge the obstacle claim, the cross-sensor plausibility check expected to detect the discrepancy, and the fallback response. An independent tracker measures the obstacle clearance and the base's motion while the camera remains disturbed. The fault record must distinguish a detected anomaly followed by a bounded stop from a missed obstacle that happened not to cause contact. If the detector cannot distinguish the disturbed signal from valid evidence, that operating condition remains a verification gap; naming a protective monitor does not establish that it will fire.

The learned proposer is itself an attack surface, and attacks on it test the proposal boundary more directly than any other fault. A vision-language-action model takes its instruction and its camera images as inputs, so an adversary can steer it through either channel without touching a bus or a sensor. Robey and colleagues automated the search for prompts that led robots controlled by language models, among them a commercial quadruped queried only as a black box, to carry out harmful actions their safeguards were meant to refuse, in many settings on every behavior they tested [@robey2025jailbreaking]. On the visual side, a small adversarial patch[^fn-adversarial-patch-camera] placed in a VLA's camera view reduced task success in simulated manipulation by as much as the entire success rate [@wang2025exploring]. For the running machine, the injection points are the task instruction and any label, sign, or printed surface inside the intent model's view. The permission path never reads the instruction, so it cannot tell a steered proposal from an honest one. It catches an injected proposal only when the resulting motion violates a quantity it measures: speed and force ceilings, stopping reserve, occupancy of the swept volume, evidence freshness, and the lease. A steered proposal that stays inside those bounds passes, whether it picks the wrong item, sets a load down in an admissible but wrong place, or opens the cage door when no task called for it, because the permission path enforces physical feasibility, not task meaning (@sec-intent-failure-modes). This is the strongest modern case for keeping proposal and permission separate: the protective claim holds however the proposal was produced, while the service claim does not. The proposer-injection row of @tbl-15-fault-classification therefore scores the trial on the physical oracle alone and records every wrong action that stayed reachable inside the envelope as a coverage deficit, not as a detected fault.

[^fn-adversarial-patch-camera]: **Adversarial Patch**\index{Adversarial patch!physical attack}: @brown2017adversarial printed a single image-independent patch that, placed anywhere in a photographed scene, made an image classifier ignore the other objects and report the attacker's chosen class. The attack reaches the model through its camera and needs access to no file, bus, or packet. For the running machine that places it entirely on the proposer's side of the proposal boundary, where the permission path can bound what a steered proposal does but cannot see the patch that steered it.

### Choosing the injection phase {#sec-verification-fault-optimization}

A stall just after renewal exercises almost the full remaining lease; a stall near expiry exercises the transition between proposal and fallback. The campaign records the injection phase rather than treating repeated injections as equivalent. Automated search can later vary phase, duration, and intensity using the oracle's measured margin (@sec-verification-falsification-trajectory-formulation).

### Compound faults and coupled disturbances {#sec-verification-compound-faults}

Each row of @tbl-15-fault-classification injects one disturbance, yet a machine in operation rarely meets one at a time. Combining rows at random would multiply the list without finding the combinations that matter, so coupled disturbances are enumerated from shared causes instead. The test ledger of the placement record (@sec-placement-hardware-allocation) names every resource that the permission path shares with the learned workloads, and each shared rail, clock, or bus becomes one compound fault, injected at the cause rather than at its symptoms.

On the running machine the clearest shared cause is the drive bus, which feeds the drives directly and the application processor through a converter, while the permission path runs from its own held-up rail. Notebook \ref{nbk-verification-supply-headroom} sizes both F4 trials from the machine's supply values.

::: {#nbk-verification-supply-headroom .callout-notebook title="The supply headroom"}

**Problem**: At the depleted point, can the drive transient alone carry the shared bus below the lockout of the converter that feeds the application processor, and how much of the permission rail's hold-up does the longest stop the enforcer can admit spend?

**Variables**:

* Depleted bus $V_{\text{low}} =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_low_str` and converter lockout $V_{\text{UVLO}} =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_uvlo_str` (Datasheet).
* Source and harness resistance $R =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_r_str` (Illustrative; needs a measured value) and drive transient $I =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.i_rail_str` (Illustrative).
* Rail hold-up `{python} RackEndVerification.rail_holdup_str` (Chosen) and spring-brake engagement $t_{\text{engage}} =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.brake_engage_str` (Illustrative).
* Longest admitted stop: from the `{python} RackEndVerification.ceiling_insp_str` inspected-floor ceiling at $a =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.a_insp_str` (Derived from the floor friction) with $j_{\max} =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.j_brake_str` m/s³ (Derived).

**Math**:

*F4a, sag under the transient and the step that reaches lockout.*
`{python} RackEndVerification.sag_math`

*F4b, flag to brakes set*, with the stop time of @eq-plan-c2-stopping-suffix.
`{python} RackEndVerification.holdup_math`

**Result**: The transient leaves `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_margin_str` of headroom above the lockout, and reaching it takes a `{python} RackEndVerification.i_cross_str` step, more than twice the transient. The `{python} RackEndVerification.rail_holdup_str` hold-up outlasts the `{python} RackEndVerification.flag_to_set_str` from flag to brakes set by `{python} RackEndVerification.holdup_margin_str`.

**Systems insight**: Neither trial can rest on the commanded load. F4a must step the supply itself, because the drive's own current cannot reach the lockout, and F4b must open the feed during the longest stop the enforcer admits, since a shorter stop passes on hold-up the claim never needed. The headroom rests on an illustrative resistance and would vanish near `{python} RackEndVerification.r_cross_str`, about twice that value, so the source resistance measured under load is the first number the supply campaign must supply.

:::

A compound trial must measure the delivered waveform and the effects on the proposer, sensors, drive logic, and independent witnesses. It cannot infer simultaneous resets or frozen frames from the commanded load alone.

A droop on a shared rail can slow the enforcer, freeze a sensor at a plausible value, and reset the logger in the same interval. A burst on a shared bus ages observations while it delays the permission path's own reads and the heartbeat that would reveal the delay. A fault in a shared clock skews the timestamps of every record that crosses the proposal boundary at once, so freshness checks pass on data that is already old. The oracle for a compound fault therefore checks the protective response against its deadline and also checks that the evidence needed to judge that response survived the same cause; the pitfalls in @sec-verification-fallacies-pitfalls show both failing together. A shared cause that the ledger does not name cannot be enumerated this way, which is why the forward analysis of the physical machine remains a separate source of faults.

The fault list now holds inverted design claims, forward-derived physical fault classes, the four authority cases, and compound faults drawn from named shared causes. It says what to inject but not where an injection is real, and that choice decides what each trial can prove.
## The Qualification Ladder {#sec-verification-qualification-ladder}

A simulator can stall the proposer of F1 at every sampled speed and payload overnight, but it cannot sag the drive bus of F4, because the simulated bus has no converter to lock out and no microcontroller to reset. This is the digital twin delusion again, now in its engineering form: the belief that millions of passing virtual rollout assertions (`assert clearance >= 0`) in a physics engine establish safety on the embodied machine.

The gap depends on what the simulator represents. A physics simulation that omits target execution and electrical dynamics can make the following idealizations; each must be checked against the claim under test:

1. **Computation takes zero virtual time:** The simulator pauses the simulation clock while the policy executes, treating heavy neural forward passes as instantaneous and decoupling inference latency from physical velocity ($d = v \tau_{\text{delay}}$).
2. **Memory bandwidth is infinite:** Tensors pass across shared in-memory references, omitting the shared-memory contention, cache evictions, and DMA serialization stalls that characterize an edge SoC.
3. **Power rails are infinitely stiff:** Supplies are modeled as constant voltages ($V = \text{const}$), ignoring the $\Delta V = I R$ sag of the drive bus under a current step (@sec-body-power-integrity; sized for this machine in \ref{nbk-verification-supply-headroom}), the inductive spikes of fast current edges, and the brownout resets either can cause.
4. **Clocks are perfectly synchronized:** The simulation advances via a single discrete time-step ($\Delta t$), eliminating real-world clock drift, interrupt jitter, and transceiver races between the neural host and the safety microcontroller.
5. **Contact mechanics are simplified:** Contact solvers approximate Coulomb friction, with linearized friction cones or with soft and convex relaxations that permit small creep under static load [@todorov2014convex], and usually omit the difference between static and kinetic friction, tire slip dynamics, and brake-lining glazing under repeated stops.

Each qualification environment closes, breaks, or substitutes different links of the loop running from sensing through inference, buses, drives, and plant. The **qualification ladder**\index{Qualification ladder!definition}\index{Four-stage qualification ladder!definition} orders four such environments, software-in-the-loop, processor-in-the-loop (PIL), hardware-in-the-loop (HIL), and physical fault rigs, by how much of that loop is real, and therefore by falling trial throughput. The order is not a hierarchy of evidence, because a higher rung cannot subsume a lower one. Each yields a distinct category of evidence while remaining blind to the physical mechanisms outside its boundary (@fig-15-qualification-ladder), so extensive software-in-the-loop passes say nothing about the clock drift, DMA stalls, interrupt jitter, or supply sag of the embedded hardware.

### Causal loop fidelity across the four rungs {#sec-verification-qualification-rungs}

@Tbl-15-qualification-ladder gives each rung's substrate, the faults it can inject, its throughput, and where its evidence ends. For the mobile manipulator, software-in-the-loop\index{Software-in-the-loop} evidence ends at the plant model, where a brake modeled as a first-order lag has no lining temperature, tire slip, or torque limit. Processor-in-the-loop (PIL)\index{Processor-in-the-loop} adds the cross-compiled binary on target silicon and so tests quantization and stack headroom; hardware-in-the-loop (HIL)\index{Hardware-in-the-loop} benches put the two-processor implementation of @sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning, its fieldbus, supplies, and drive stages against an FPGA plant or a dynamometer; and physical fault rigs\index{In-situ physical fault rigs} add the production base, brakes, harness, and floor. Two sources beside the ladder open the loop altogether. Trace replay keeps real sensor noise but supplies the frames that followed the original command rather than the new one. Shadow operation runs the candidate beside an incumbent controller, so if the candidate proposes a velocity that would carry the base past a rack end, its log records the command while the incumbent keeps the base where it belongs. Neither shows the physical consequence of a command.

A shadow deployment cannot let a stalled proposer drive the base toward a rack end that may hold a person, a simulator cannot reveal a race in transceiver silicon, and a hardware bench cannot run the millions of randomized runs that tail statistics need. Each fault injection therefore goes to the rung that exercises its causal mechanism.

::: {#fig-15-qualification-ladder fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**What each rung makes real**: A filled cell is the production item itself, a dashed cell is a model standing in for it, and a dash marks a link the rung idealizes away. Coverage of the causal loop grows down the ladder while trial throughput falls, so no rung dominates. A mechanism can fail only on a rung that contains it, and only the rungs near the top are cheap enough to search at scale." fig-alt="Matrix with four rows, software-in-the-loop, PIL, HIL, and physical rig, and six columns: decision logic, execution timing, bus and I/O timing, supply transients, drives and brakes, and contact and floor. The software-in-the-loop row fills only decision logic, shows drives and floor as models, and leaves the other three columns empty. PIL adds execution timing, shows the bus as a model, and leaves supply transients empty. HIL fills every column except contact and floor, which it shows as a model. The physical rig fills all six. A right-hand column lists throughput falling from parallel sweeps through target-bound and real time to wall clock limited by wear."}
![](images/svg/fig15_qualification_ladder.svg){width="95%"}
:::

The choice of rung follows the failed premise. F1 needs target execution to test lease expiry under processor interference; F4 needs the production supply path and independent rail measurements. A stopping-distance claim also needs the loaded body and qualified floor. We can use simulation to select challenging conditions, then reproduce those conditions on the rung that contains the mechanism under test. Agreement between rungs supports only the mechanisms represented in both; the table records the remaining limits.

| Qualification Rung & Substrate                                     | Causal Loop Realism (Compute, Bus, Actuator, Plant)                                                                                                          | Fault Injection Mechanism & Scope                                                          | Throughput & Sample Scaling                                         | Physical & Temporal Fidelity                                                            | Primary Test Oracle & Evidentiary Limit                                                                                                                                                  |
|:-------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Software-in-the-Loop** (Host Workstation / Cloud Cluster)        | **Compute:** Synthetic / Host x86; **Bus:** Idealized zero-copy buffer; **Actuator:** Linear / saturation model; **Plant:** Numerical ODE/PDE solver         | Tensor bit-flips, synthetic sensor dropout, floor-friction, payload, and latency sweeps    | Parallel sweeps; throughput depends on model and compute allocation | High mathematical flexibility; zero target silicon, bus timing, or electrical realism   | **Oracle:** Mathematical assertion corridors and state invariants. **Limit:** Cannot validate target execution timing or unmodeled physical dynamics.                                    |
| **Processor-in-the-Loop (PIL)** (Target SoC / MCU Core Emulation)  | **Compute:** Real target silicon (ARM/RISC-V); **Bus:** Simulated bus interconnect; **Actuator:** Emulated command register; **Plant:** Real-time host model | Instruction cache evictions, register corruption via JTAG/BIST, interrupt jitter injection | Bound by target execution and cross-platform synchronization        | Instruction-set and compiler accurate; abstracts analog bus lines and actuator back-EMF | **Oracle:** Target register state, numerical equivalence, and execution-time profiles. **Limit:** Ignores physical transceiver bus contention, voltage droop, and thermal rise.          |
| **Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL)** (Target ECUs + Real-Time Plant Rig) | **Compute:** Production ECU / NPU; **Bus:** Real physical CAN/Ethernet; **Actuator:** Real motor drives / dyno; **Plant:** Hard real-time FPGA plant rig     | Pin break/short, CAN frame stuffing / babbling idiot, supply rail droop, load steps        | $1.0\times$ strict real-time ($24\text{ h/day}$ wall-clock limit)   | High electrical, timing, and protocol fidelity; bounded by FPGA plant model accuracy    | **Oracle:** Protocol CRC, bus deadline monitors, and interlock timings. **Limit:** Cannot execute destructive physical overload or simulate tire and lining wear.                        |
| **Physical Fault Rig** (Dynamometer Cell / Field Plant)            | **Compute:** Production ECU / NPU; **Bus:** Production harness & sensors; **Actuator:** Real physical mechanisms; **Plant:** Real base, arm, and floor       | Wheel clamps, magnetic brake stall, thermal heating, transducer bias drift                 | Wall-clock execution; constrained by wear and thermal reset         | Full authentic physics (Coulomb friction, wheel slip, thermal dissipation, wear)        | **Oracle:** Independent physical containment instrumentation and yield transducers. **Limit:** High financial cost per trial; destructive tests cannot scale to statistical tail bounds. |

: **The four-stage qualification ladder across cyber-physical boundaries**: The four qualification environments compared by computing substrate, exercised causal-loop elements, fault injection primitives, execution throughput, physical and temporal fidelity, and test oracle. {#tbl-15-qualification-ladder tbl-colwidths="[16,22,16,14,16,16]"}

### The causal loop coverage rule and evidentiary limits {#sec-verification-qualification-limits}

The fidelity boundary of a test environment is where a model, an emulated bus, or a replayed trace severs the exchange of energy and information between computation and mechanics (@sec-boundary-causal-boundary). Physical wire harnesses, ground returns, and distributed actuator units cannot be replaced by idealized desktop simulations without omitting inductive voltage droop, transmission reflections, and EMI coupling. No qualification rung can certify properties outside its causal boundary. Software-in-the-loop runs falsify algorithmic logic. PIL falsifies numerical and compiler equivalence on the target and profiles execution, but it exchanges I/O over a debug or serial link, so timing under real I/O needs HIL. HIL falsifies bus contention, I/O timing, and electrical transients, and physical rigs falsify contact mechanics and thermal dissipation.

A higher rung therefore does not subsume or obsolete the lower ones. Test engineering is an optimization problem under resource constraints: parallel software-in-the-loop runs can explore many combinations of lighting and obstacle conditions, whereas physical rigs exercise actual contact mechanics and require reset, inspection, and thermal recovery between trials. Each stage occupies a unique point on the Pareto frontier balancing combinatorial test throughput against physical causal fidelity. A mechanism the model omits cannot fail in it. A joint with unmodeled Coulomb breakaway friction and stator lag sits still for a dead time the simulator never shows and then trails the simulated trajectory, an instance of the omitted-mechanism class of @sec-training-sim-to-real-gap that only a rung with the real joint can expose.

To prevent false confidence, every reported verification result must explicitly state which elements of the causal loop were physically real, which were simulated, which were replayed from static logs, which were bypassed, and which remained unobserved. A claim that the permission path stopped the base within `{python} RackEndVerification.budget_str` means nothing without specifying whether the wheel-speed signal was generated by a differential equation, read from a physical encoder over the real fieldbus, or replayed from a digital buffer. Specifying this causal mapping exposes the assumptions underlying each test, so that unmodeled physics cannot hide a latent hazard.

### Scope of a formal verification result {#sec-verification-formal-limits}

```{python}
#| label: calc-verify-nn-scale
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ NEURAL-NETWORK VERIFICATION SCALE AGAINST THE RUNNING MACHINE'S PROPOSER (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-verification-formal-limits, @tbl-15-verification-state-of-practice.
# │ Goal: Compare the largest network scored in VNN-COMP 2025 with the running
# │       machine's intent model, to motivate verifying the permission path.
# │ Show: 138 million parameters; the 7B proposer is about 51x larger.
# │ How: ratio of parameter counts.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Embodied
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_params, fmt_multiple, check

class NNVerificationScale:
    """Scale of complete NN verification (as of 2025) against the machine's proposer."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    proposer_params = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator.intent_model.parameters  # category: datasheet
    # Largest scored network in VNN-COMP 2025 (VGGNet16 benchmark), @kaulen2025vnncomp; category: sourced
    vnn_max_params = 138e6 * ureg.param

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    ratio = float((proposer_params / vnn_max_params).to("dimensionless").magnitude)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(ratio > 10, "The proposer must exceed the largest verified benchmark by more than an order of magnitude.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    vnn_max_params_str = fmt_params(vnn_max_params, precision=0)
    proposer_params_str = fmt_params(proposer_params, precision=0)
    ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(ratio), precision=0)  # displayed as "about"
```

A formal proof is a further source of evidence beside the four rungs, and like each rung it has a boundary. A proof for the permission mechanism can establish a property over its modeled states and disturbances. Its application to the machine still depends on the plant model, observations, execution deadlines, and available actuation. The question for this machine is which component a proof can reach, and the state of neural-network verification answers it.

A neural-network verifier checks an **open-loop property**\index{Neural network verification!open-loop property}: for every input in a specified set, such as all images within a small perturbation of a nominal frame, the network's output satisfies a specified condition. Two mechanisms do the work. **Bound propagation**\index{Bound propagation} pushes the input set through the network layer by layer, replacing each nonlinear activation with linear upper and lower bounds, and returns a sound but possibly loose enclosure of the outputs; if the enclosure already satisfies the condition, the property holds. When it does not, **branch and bound**\index{Branch and bound!neural network verification} splits an unstable activation into its two linear pieces and bounds each half again, so the search is complete in principle and exponential in the number of splits in the worst case. Reluplex [@katz2017reluplex] and its successor Marabou [@wu2024marabou] reach completeness through a constraint solver instead; the α,β-CROWN verifier combines GPU-accelerated bound propagation with branch and bound [@xu2021alphacrown; @wang2021betacrown].

A **closed-loop property**\index{Neural network verification!closed-loop property} is a different object. It asks whether the state of a plant driven by a network controller stays inside a safe set over a horizon, so the verifier must compose the network's output bounds with the plant dynamics at every step and control the growth of the reachable set. Tools such as NNV, Verisig, and POLAR do this for small controllers and low-dimensional plants [@tran2020nnv; @ivanov2019verisig; @huang2022polar]. None of them takes camera frames as input: their state is the plant's few physical variables, which is exactly the form of the permission path's inputs and not the form of a vision-language-action policy's.

@Tbl-15-verification-state-of-practice dates the scale at which these tools operate. The largest network in the 2025 international verification competition had `{python} NNVerificationScale.vnn_max_params_str` parameters, and most scored benchmarks were far smaller [@kaulen2025vnncomp]. The running machine's `{python} NNVerificationScale.proposer_params_str`-parameter chunk policy is about `{python} NNVerificationScale.ratio_mult_str` larger than that outlier, takes a stream of images rather than a bounded input set, and has no specification of the form "for all inputs in this set" that would mean anything at the rack end. Complete verification of the proposer is therefore out of reach, and the obstacle is the missing specification as much as the scale. That is the argument for the architecture this book has built since @sec-boundary: the learned proposer is evaluated, while the small permission path, whose inputs are a handful of physical quantities and whose property is a stopping invariant, is the part a proof can reach.

| Method class                       | Representative tool                                                       | What a result establishes                                                                    | Scale and limit, as of 2026                                                                                                                        |
|:-----------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Complete open-loop NN verification | α,β-CROWN [@wang2021betacrown]; Marabou 2.0 [@wu2024marabou]              | A property holds for every input in a bounded set, or a counterexample input                 | α,β-CROWN ranked first in VNN-COMP 2025; scored benchmarks reach `{python} NNVerificationScale.vnn_max_params_str` parameters [@kaulen2025vnncomp] |
| Closed-loop reachability           | NNV [@tran2020nnv]; Verisig [@ivanov2019verisig]; POLAR [@huang2022polar] | The plant state under a network controller stays in a safe set over a horizon                | Small controllers and low-dimensional plants; sets grow conservative over long horizons                                                            |
| STL falsification                  | S-TaLiRo [@annpureddy2011staliro]; Breach [@donze2010breach]              | A counterexample trajectory with negative robustness, or none found within the search budget | Black-box simulation of any model; no certificate from an unsuccessful search                                                                      |
| Rare-event estimation              | Importance sampling with the cross-entropy method [@okelly2018scalable]   | A failure probability under a declared operational distribution, with its variance           | Only as good as the declared distribution and the proposal's coverage of the failure set                                                           |

: **Verification methods and their reach, as of 2026**: Representative tools for each method class, what a result establishes, and the scale at which it currently operates. The mechanisms in the prose are durable; the named tools and scales will change, so the table carries its date. {#tbl-15-verification-state-of-practice tbl-colwidths="[20,24,28,28]"}

High-dimensional reachability, nonlinear contact, and hybrid switching can make analysis of the permission path itself expensive or conservative. Those limits do not make every useful proof impossible. They favor a smaller, explicit permission claim whose premises can be challenged independently on the target hardware.

::: {#chk-verification-rung-choice .callout-checkpoint title="Rung choice and the reach of a proof"}

A rung, like a proof, supports only the mechanisms it contains.

- [ ] **Rung selection**: For F2 (a frame held at the image signal processor), F3 (lost fieldbus frames), and an actuator jam, can you name the lowest rung that contains the causal mechanism and one mechanism that rung still idealizes away?
- [ ] **Agreement between rungs**: Can you explain why a software-in-the-loop pass and a HIL pass on the same scenario support only the mechanisms both rungs represent?
- [ ] **Replay vs. shadow operation**: Can you explain why neither trace replay nor shadow operation shows the physical consequence of the candidate's command?
- [ ] **Proof scope**: Can you explain why a closed-loop reachability proof can reach the permission path but not the vision-language-action proposer, and list the premises such a proof leaves to physical test?

:::
## Fault Injection on Hardware {#sec-verification-hardware-fault-injection}

A fault injected in simulation tests only the modeled response. On the machine, contention on a shared bus, clock drift between microcontrollers, DMA stalls, and voltage drop across inductive drivers decide whether an intervention executes in time, and a simulator that has not represented and validated those effects leaves them outside its evidence. On an embodied machine, fault injection must therefore pass through the compute, communication, and power substrate. Injection happens on target hardware, through the real transceivers, timers, shared buses, and enforcement path, while an independent containment rig protects the test facility.

**In-situ fault injection**\index{In-situ fault injection!definition} is the deliberate, deterministic introduction of physical, electrical, and computational disturbances (including sensor register latches, clock drift, bus contention, supply brownouts, and actuator load stalls) directly into target production silicon and mechanics while operating under authentic electrical, thermal, and dynamic loads.

### Physical injection needles across sensor, bus, and power {#sec-verification-injection-needles}

A fault injected in software above the driver never exercises the interface where the physical fault enters, so a campaign places its injectors at the physical interfaces themselves.[^fn-hw-hil-needles] Four kinds cover the machine's claims:

[^fn-hw-hil-needles]: **Injection fixtures**\index{Fault injection!circuitry schematics}: Power injectors switch or program the supply with solid-state devices, and bus injectors drive the lines through high-impedance buffers. The instrumentation must be isolated from the drive's high-current transients, or the witness fails with the machine. The achievable edge rate and isolation are properties of the specific fixture and belong in the trial record.

1. *Sensor ingress injectors:* inline interposers on the camera's serial link freeze frames, delay them with their capture stamps preserved, or corrupt pixel data at the physical boundary without modifying software drivers.
2. *Fieldbus disturbance nodes:* CAN FD and EtherCAT disturbance nodes corrupt checksums, force bit collisions that drive a node into its bus-off state,[^fn-busoff-error-confinement] drop synchronization frames, and emulate a babbling idiot, a faulty node that transmits continuously and starves the others of bus time.
3. *Supply injectors:* a programmable supply standing in for the pack, together with an electronic load, steps the drive bus and the logic rails through declared waveforms. The delivered waveform is measured, because a fixture's slew-rate limit bounds which transients a trial can reproduce.
4. *Dynamometer actuator injectors:* load machines coupled to wheel hubs or arm joints command step torques that emulate bearing seizures, brake-lining glazing, or abrupt mechanical jams while the motor current response is measured.

[^fn-busoff-error-confinement]: **Bus-Off**\index{CAN!bus-off state}: CAN confines an error to the node that makes it. Each controller counts its own transmit and receive errors, and once its transmit count passes the limit the standard fixes, it disconnects itself until it has observed a long run of idle bus bits [@iso11898-1-2015], so a faulty node silences itself rather than the network. An injector that forces collisions can turn the same rule against a healthy node and remove it from the bus with no software fault at all, so the trial must show that the permission path notices the silent node within its budget.

Testing the two-processor implementation\index{Two-processor implementation!fault injection} (@sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning) demands physical fault injection at the boundaries its claims name. @Tbl-15-fault-classification gives each case's detector, response, and pass condition; the list adds how each fault is injected and, where it matters, where its events are timed:

- **Stale Observation Injection (F2):** An inline FPGA interceptor latches a navigation-camera frame at the image signal processor, or suppresses encoder updates, while preserving the original hardware timestamp. Detector assertion, powered deceleration onset, and wheel speed are measured on independent instruments.
- **Expired Lease Revocation (F1):** The test framework lets the proposer renew once and then suppresses every later renewal. Lease expiry, revocation on the enforcer's next `{python} RackEndVerification.t_tick_str` tick, and powered deceleration onset are each measured on their own wire and clock.
- **Lost-Frame Injection (F3):** A fieldbus disturbance node drops or corrupts EtherCAT frames at a drive's slave port while the base cruises, and the master's working-counter check[^fn-ethercat-working-counter] is the first detector that can see the loss. Each lost `{python} RackEndVerification.t_bus_str` cycle costs `{python} RackEndVerification.per_ms_str` of travel at the aisle speed.
- **Drive-Bus Droop and Feed-Loss Injection (F4a, F4b):** A programmable supply standing in for the pack at its `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_low_str` depleted point carries the `{python} RackEndVerification.i_rail_str` transient of hard drive acceleration with the application SoC at full load, then steps the drive bus below the `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_uvlo_str` converter lockout, which the load alone cannot reach (\ref{nbk-verification-supply-headroom}), while the permission path runs on the isolated, held-up rail that @sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder sizes and the placement record carries (@sec-placement-hardware-allocation). An independent digitizer records the permission-path heartbeat, and powered deceleration onset is timed from the undervoltage flag. F4b opens the permission rail's feed during the longest stop the enforcer can admit on an inspected floor, the resident stop from its `{python} RackEndVerification.ceiling_insp_str` ceiling. Independent measurements must also establish surviving drive authority and energy absorption throughout the powered stop. Logic hold-up alone leaves that premise open. A reset of the permission path is `FAIL` in either trial, whatever the stopping distance, because a stop that power loss hands to the spring brakes mid-motion is not the stop the claim budgets.
- **Handover Stall Injection (A3):** The testbed freezes the remote assistant's input during `PEND` and drops the acknowledgment frames at both speeds, and both fallback dispatch and physical onset at the drive are timed independently. The waiting allowance bounds dispatch; onset must also satisfy the allocated command-to-response interval.

[^fn-ethercat-working-counter]: **EtherCAT Working Counter**\index{EtherCAT!working counter}: Each slave that successfully processes a datagram increments a counter carried in the frame as it passes, so the value that returns to the master states how many addressed devices actually read or wrote their data. A dropped frame never returns and a corrupted one returns with a short count, both within the cycle in which they were sent, which is why F3 can be detected at the master one bus cycle after the loss instead of waiting for a drive's communication watchdog to expire.

The duplicate writer (A1), the tier bypass (A2), and the replayed or forged packet (A4) need no fixture beyond a second bus master and a packet injector on the testbed, and are injected as @tbl-15-fault-classification states. The four injectors and the instruments that witness them fit on one bench, and the layout of @fig-15-f1-test-rig follows from the rule that no instrument may share a clock or a supply with the machine it scores.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ VALUES DRAWN IN THE F1 TEST-RIG FIGURE (LEGO)
# │ Context: @fig-15-f1-test-rig (fig15_f1_test_rig.svg)
# │ Goal:    keep the hand-drawn supply and hold-up labels pinned to the oracle cell
# │ Show:    47.7 V bus, 33 V lockout, 37.8 V sag, 4.8 V headroom, 150 A step,
# │          2.0 s hold-up, 1,313 ms flag to brakes set, 1 kHz permission tick
# │ How:     check() each drawn label against RackEndVerification
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

class VerificationRigFigure:
    """Values drawn in fig15_f1_test_rig.svg."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    R = RackEndVerification  # category: derived; calc in @sec-verification-fault-injection

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    for _q, _unit, _drawn, _tol in (
        (R.bus_nominal, ureg.volt, 47.7, 5e-3),
        (R.bus_uvlo, ureg.volt, 33.0, 1e-9),
        (R.bus_min, ureg.volt, 37.8, 5e-3),
        (R.bus_margin, ureg.volt, 4.8, 5e-3),
        (R.i_cross, ureg.ampere, 150.0, 1e-6),
        (R.rail_holdup, second, 2.0, 1e-9),
        (R.flag_to_set, millisecond, 1313.0, 0.5),
        (R.t_tick, millisecond, 1.0, 1e-9),
    ):
        check(abs(_q.to(_unit).magnitude - _drawn) < _tol, f"test-rig figure label {_drawn} is stale")

```

### Timing faults across clock domains {#sec-verification-hardware-timing-search}

Camera capture, proposal generation, permission ticks, and fieldbus cycles run on different clocks. A reproducible test records the disturbance's phase relative to each relevant event. Sweeping those phases challenges races that an injection at one fixed phase cannot reach; searching them does not establish that the worst case has been found.

Consider F2 on the hardware. The navigation camera stamps each frame at capture, and the frame's age at dispatch is budgeted at `{python} RackEndVerification.t_age_str` (@sec-perception-transduction-calibration). At `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` the base covers `{python} RackEndVerification.per_ms_str` in every millisecond, so an unaccounted delay spends the reserve directly. The `{python} RackEndVerification.upper_age_str` upper-age value applies at dispatch; the evidence continues aging during admission and execution. A per-tick test must use the remaining stopping budget and the active command's validity, not reset age at dispatch or reuse that dispatch threshold as a universal live limit. Left undetected for `{python} RackEndVerification.t_spare_str`, it consumes all `{python} RackEndVerification.spare_str`. Neither the camera's datasheet readout time nor the timestamp on a single frame establishes how quickly the permission path notices. A measured $P_{99}$ detection time leaves the worst case unbounded (@sec-nervous-deterministic-fieldbuses), so the containment claim needs a detection bound justified over the declared compute-load, bus-load, and thermal envelope.

```{python}
#| label: calc-verify-clock-drift
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CLOCK-CONVERSION DRIFT AGAINST THE F2 BOUND (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: hardware fault-injection section, @eq-verification-clock-drift.
# │ Goal: Show how quickly oscillator drift between the application processor
# │       and the safety microcontroller spends the 0.2 ms clock-conversion
# │       bound that F2's refusal threshold rests on, and what a sync blackout costs.
# │ Show: 200 ppm worst relative rate; bound consumed after 1 s unsynchronized;
# │       20 us per 100 ms sync period; 80 us over a four-period blackout, 95 us
# │       with one sigma of jitter; 100 us after a fifth missed period.
# │ How: drift = rate x elapsed time; allowance = RackEndVerification.eps_sync.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import microsecond, millisecond, second
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt_latency, check

class ClockDriftVerification:
    """Oscillator drift between the two processors, tested against the clock-conversion bound."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    ppm_ap = 100  # application-processor oscillator limit, ppm; scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    ppm_mcu = 50  # safety-microcontroller oscillator limit, ppm; scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    ppm_thermal = 50  # separately bounded thermal contribution, ppm; scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    t_sync = 100 * millisecond  # healthy sync period; scenario assumption; category: chosen
    n_blackout = 4  # sync periods between two good frames (three dropped); scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    sigma_jitter = 15 * microsecond  # observed sync jitter, one standard deviation; scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    eps_sync = RackEndVerification.eps_sync  # clock-conversion bound of the observation contract; category: derived

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    ppm_total = ppm_ap + ppm_mcu + ppm_thermal
    rate = ppm_total * microsecond / second  # worst relative drift rate
    t_consume = (eps_sync / rate).to(second)
    drift_period = (rate * t_sync).to(microsecond)
    t_blackout = (n_blackout * t_sync).to(millisecond)
    drift_blackout = (rate * t_blackout).to(microsecond)
    one_sigma = (drift_blackout + sigma_jitter).to(microsecond)
    drift_fifth = (rate * (n_blackout + 1) * t_sync).to(microsecond)
    fifth_share = float((drift_fifth / eps_sync).to("dimensionless").magnitude)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(ppm_total == 200, "Worst relative rate must be 200 ppm.")
    check(abs(t_consume.magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "Drift alone must consume the 0.2 ms bound after 1 s.")
    check(abs(drift_blackout.magnitude - 80.0) < 1e-9, "Four-period blackout must drift 80 us.")
    check(one_sigma < eps_sync.to(microsecond), "The one-sigma scenario must sit inside the conversion bound.")
    check(abs(fifth_share - 0.5) < 1e-9, "A fifth missed period must spend half the bound.")
    # margin_sync_blackout_drift_envelope.svg fig-alt hand-types 80, 95, 100, and 200 us
    check(
        abs(one_sigma.to(microsecond).magnitude - 95.0) < 1e-9 and abs(drift_fifth.to(microsecond).magnitude - 100.0) < 1e-9,
        "Clock-envelope fig-alt: 95 us one-sigma, 100 us fifth period.",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    ppm_ap_str = fmt_int(ppm_ap)
    ppm_mcu_str = fmt_int(ppm_mcu)
    ppm_thermal_str = fmt_int(ppm_thermal)
    ppm_total_str = fmt_int(ppm_total)
    t_consume_str = fmt_latency(t_consume, unit=second, precision=0)
    t_sync_str = fmt_latency(t_sync, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    drift_period_str = fmt_latency(drift_period, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_blackout_str = fmt_latency(t_blackout, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    drift_blackout_str = fmt_latency(drift_blackout, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    sigma_jitter_str = fmt_latency(sigma_jitter, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    one_sigma_str = fmt_latency(one_sigma, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    drift_fifth_str = fmt_latency(drift_fifth, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
```

### Distributed clock drift and synchronization blackouts {#sec-verification-clock-drift-sync}

Testing distributed loops exposes clock-conversion risk even when each processor meets its local schedule. F2's refusal threshold rests on the `{python} RackEndVerification.eps_sync_str` bound for converting a capture stamp to the safety microcontroller's clock, and that bound is itself a claim to test. Take illustrative oscillator limits of ±`{python} ClockDriftVerification.ppm_ap_str` ppm on the application processor and ±`{python} ClockDriftVerification.ppm_mcu_str` ppm on the safety microcontroller, plus a separately bounded `{python} ClockDriftVerification.ppm_thermal_str` ppm thermal contribution that those specifications do not include. The worst relative rate is then `{python} ClockDriftVerification.ppm_total_str` ppm, and drift alone would consume the `{python} RackEndVerification.eps_sync_str` bound after `{python} ClockDriftVerification.t_consume_str` without resynchronization. A healthy `{python} ClockDriftVerification.t_sync_str` sync period limits that drift contribution to `{python} ClockDriftVerification.drift_period_str`; network and conversion error must be budgeted separately.

Suppose two good sync frames arrive `{python} ClockDriftVerification.t_blackout_str` apart while the three scheduled frames between them are dropped. The blackout lasts four sync periods, and the bounded drift contribution grows to `{python} ClockDriftVerification.drift_blackout_str`. If the observed synchronization jitter has standard deviation $\sigma_{\text{jitter}}$ = `{python} ClockDriftVerification.sigma_jitter_str`, adding one sigma to the drift rate $r_{\text{drift}}$ times the blackout $T_{\text{blackout}}$ gives
$$\Delta t_{\text{one-sigma scenario}}=r_{\text{drift}}\,T_{\text{blackout}}+\sigma_{\text{jitter}}$$ {#eq-verification-clock-drift}
or `{python} ClockDriftVerification.one_sigma_str`. The one-sigma value in @eq-verification-clock-drift is not a hard bound; a deterministic deadline needs a justified jitter envelope and a clock-conversion test. A fifth elapsed period, with four intervening sync frames dropped, gives `{python} ClockDriftVerification.drift_fifth_str` of drift alone, before jitter, half the `{python} RackEndVerification.eps_sync_str` bound on which F2's threshold rests. If clock drift and synchronization jitter combine to breach that bound, two symmetric physical failure modes jeopardize the machine. On one hand, a completely fresh camera frame may appear artificially aged when evaluated against the safety microcontroller's drifted clock, causing the enforcer to falsely reject valid proposals and trip an unprompted emergency stop, stranding the base in an active warehouse aisle. On the other hand, a dangerously delayed observation may appear falsely fresh, duping the permission path into executing proposals computed from obsolete obstacle coordinates while the loaded base cruises at `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` toward a closed aisle gate.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_sync_blackout_drift_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Bars of clock-conversion drift against a dashed 200 microsecond bound: 80 microseconds after a four-period sync blackout, 95 microseconds with one sigma of jitter added, and 100 microseconds after a fifth period."}

*Five missed sync periods spend half the clock-conversion bound.*
:::

Every injection on the hardware ends with the same obligation. The detector that fired, the moment of refusal, the takeover at the drive, and the physical outcome are measured on instruments the fault cannot reach, on one reference clock, and a trial that loses any of them has not shown what it set out to show. The hardware campaign therefore produces records rather than a pass count, each binding one trial to its claim, its envelope point, its builds, and its evidence.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Hardware-in-the-loop stress results furnish the evidentiary warrants for safety cases in @sec-release-safety-cases-claims.
:::
## Searching Beyond the First Trial {#sec-verification-search-campaign}

The F1 specification establishes a reproducible question, witness, and verdict rule. Finding less obvious failures requires varying the conditions and measuring how close each run comes to its limits. These searches prioritize tests; they do not replace the coverage record.

### Signal temporal logic and quantitative robustness {#sec-verification-stl-robustness}

Temporal logic entered program verification when @pnueli1977temporal used it to specify how a program's states must unfold over time, not only what the program computes. **Signal Temporal Logic (STL)** carries the idea to dense time and real-valued signals, combining physical predicates with real-time conditions such as always remaining within a distance bound or eventually stopping before a deadline [@maler2004monitoring] (@sec-appendix-ml-stl). These requirements admit **quantitative robustness semantics**\index{Quantitative robustness semantics!definition} [@fainekos2009robustness]. Instead of a simple binary pass/fail boolean flag, robustness is a continuous real-valued metric $\rho(\phi, s, t) \in \mathbb{R}$ that measures *how far* a real-valued signal trajectory $s: \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} \to \mathbb{R}^n$ remains from violating or satisfying a temporal requirement $\phi$ at time $t$.

For an atomic physical predicate $\pi \equiv (f(s(t)) \ge 0)$ (such as spatial clearance $d(t) - d_{\text{safe}} \ge 0$), quantitative robustness evaluates the signed predicate margin: $\rho(\pi, s, t) = f(s(t))$. Across temporal horizons, safety invariants evaluate worst-case (minimum) margin, while eventual deadlines evaluate the best-case (maximum):
$$\rho(\square_{[0, T]} \phi, s, 0) = \min_{t \in [0, T]} \rho(\phi, s, t), \qquad \rho(\lozenge_{[0, \tau]} \phi, s, 0) = \max_{t \in [0, \tau]} \rho(\phi, s, t).$$ {#eq-verification-stl-recursive-robustness}
Here $\square_{[0,T]}$ reads "always on $[0,T]$" and $\lozenge_{[0,\tau]}$ reads "eventually within $\tau$."

The sign and magnitude of $\rho$ in @eq-verification-stl-recursive-robustness establish an immediate operational interpretation:
$$\rho > 0 \implies \text{satisfied with positive margin } \rho, \qquad \rho < 0 \implies \text{violated with shortfall depth } |\rho|.$$
For example, if the clearance margin is $\rho = +0.15\,\text{m}$, the minimum clearance along the trajectory exceeded the required clearance by 15 centimeters; if $\rho = -0.04\,\text{m}$, the machine breached the specified clearance by 4 centimeters, and whether contact occurred depends on how that clearance was defined.

This value margin is **space robustness**\index{Space robustness}: how far the signal's value could move before the verdict changes. It does not measure lateness. A deadline violation is a margin in time, and **time robustness**\index{Time robustness} is a separate semantics that asks how far the signal could shift in time before the verdict changes [@donze2010robust]. The two answer different questions and should not be mixed inside one formula. For F1 the simplest correct treatment keeps the onset deadline outside the STL formula, as a scalar predicate on the measured onset time, and scores the distance requirement with space robustness.

The F1 oracle therefore has two parts. Powered deceleration must begin within `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str` of the last successful lease renewal, and travel from that same event must remain within `{python} RackEndVerification.f1_aisle_stop_bound_str` at the aisle speed, a space-robustness predicate on position. A different reference event requires a different distance bound.

For a numerical illustration, take one F1 trace at the aisle speed whose powered deceleration onset comes `{python} RackEndVerification.late_onset_str` late, at `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_late_str` after the last valid renewal. The onset margin against the `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str` bound is `{python} RackEndVerification.rho_onset_str`. The base covers `{python} RackEndVerification.late_extra_str` more before braking begins, so travel from renewal to rest reaches `{python} RackEndVerification.travel_late_str` and the distance margin against the `{python} RackEndVerification.f1_aisle_stop_bound_str` oracle is `{python} RackEndVerification.rho_dist_str`. Both predicates fail, and the record reports both in their own units. A minimum taken across milliseconds and millimeters means nothing, so combining them into one score with `min` requires each margin first to be divided by a predeclared positive scale in its own unit; the record keeps the raw margins and the scales, so that the combined verdict remains physically interpretable. With scales chosen equal to the bounds themselves, the normalized margins are `{python} RackEndVerification.rho_onset_n_str` for onset and `{python} RackEndVerification.rho_dist_n_str` for distance, so the onset predicate sets the combined score. A different choice of scales would change which predicate dominates, which is why the scales are fixed before the trial. These values are model arithmetic on a stipulated trace, not measurements.

::: {#fig-15-hardware-fault-injection fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**One F1 trace against its oracle**: Model timelines, not measurements, of the channels an F1 trial must witness at `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str`, timed from the last valid renewal. The execution lease expires at `{python} RackEndVerification.t_lease_str`, the next permission tick commands the stop, the fieldbus delivers it, and powered deceleration must begin by `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str`; a proposal probed after expiry is refused. The dashed trace brakes `{python} RackEndVerification.late_onset_str` late, so its onset margin is `{python} RackEndVerification.rho_onset_str` and its `{python} RackEndVerification.travel_late_str` of travel overruns the `{python} RackEndVerification.f1_aisle_stop_bound_str` oracle by `{python} RackEndVerification.rho_dist_str`." fig-alt="Two stacked panels sharing time after the last valid renewal. The upper panel, from 0 to 130 milliseconds, shows five logic channels, each labeled with its witness instrument: proposer renewals with a pulse at 0, a task-killed mark just after it, and a refused probe at 65 ms; the execution lease high until it expires at 60 ms; the stop command rising at the next tick, 61 ms; the drive frame rising at 62 ms; and powered deceleration rising at the 82 ms bound in green, with a dashed red trace rising at 112 ms and a 30 ms onset margin marked between them. A shaded onset allowance spans 62 to 82 ms. The lower panel, from 0 to about 1,200 ms, shows base speed falling in an S-curve from 1.3 m/s to rest at 1,013 ms for the green trace, 751.9 mm of travel, and at 1,043 ms for the dashed red trace, 790.9 mm and a margin of minus 39 mm."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ONE F1 TRACE AGAINST ITS ORACLE (FIGURE)
# │ Context: @fig-15-hardware-fault-injection
# │ Goal:    show the channels an F1 trial must witness, to scale, against the
# │          renewal-referenced oracle
# │ Show:    lease expiry 60 ms, stop command at the next tick, fieldbus frame,
# │          onset bound 82 ms and a late onset at 112 ms; base speed from
# │          1.3 m/s to rest with 751.9 and 790.9 mm of travel
# │ How:     event times from RackEndVerification; jerk-limited stop profile from
# │          calc_scurve_stop_time and the chapter's a_brake and j_brake
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.fmt import check
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_scurve_stop_time

R = RackEndVerification

# ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
v0 = R.v_aisle.to(meter / second).magnitude  # category: chosen
a = R.a_brake.to(meter / second**2).magnitude  # category: illustrative
j = R.j_brake.to(meter / second**3).magnitude  # category: derived
t_lease = R.t_lease.to(millisecond).magnitude
t_cmd = (R.t_lease + R.t_tick).to(millisecond).magnitude
t_frame = (R.t_lease + R.t_tick + R.t_bus).to(millisecond).magnitude
t_onset = R.onset_bound.to(millisecond).magnitude
t_late = R.onset_late.to(millisecond).magnitude
t_probe = R.lease_probe_at.to(millisecond).magnitude

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
T_stop = calc_scurve_stop_time(R.v_aisle, R.a_brake, R.j_brake).to(second).magnitude
T1 = a / j  # jerk ramp
T2 = T_stop - 2 * T1  # constant-deceleration phase

def speed(t_ms, onset_ms):
    """Base speed of the jerk-limited resident stop entered at onset_ms."""
    s = np.clip((np.asarray(t_ms) - onset_ms) / 1000.0, 0.0, None)
    v = np.where(s <= T1, v0 - 0.5 * j * s**2, 0.0)
    v1 = v0 - 0.5 * j * T1**2
    v = np.where((s > T1) & (s <= T1 + T2), v1 - a * (s - T1), v)
    s3 = s - T1 - T2
    v2 = v1 - a * T2
    v = np.where((s > T1 + T2) & (s <= T_stop), v2 - a * s3 + 0.5 * j * s3**2, v)
    return np.maximum(v, 0.0)

t = np.linspace(0.0, 1200.0, 24001)
v_bound = speed(t, t_onset)
v_late = speed(t, t_late)
d_stop_mm = np.trapezoid(np.where(t >= t_onset, v_bound, 0.0), t / 1000.0) * 1000.0

# ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(d_stop_mm - R.c2_distance.magnitude) < 0.5, "Plotted S-curve stop must integrate to the chapter's stop distance.")
check(abs(t_onset - 82.0) < 1e-9 and abs(t_late - 112.0) < 1e-9, "Trace onsets are 82 ms and 112 ms.")
check(abs(t_probe - 65.0) < 1e-9, "The post-expiry probe is at 65 ms.")

# ┌── 4. PLOT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
viz.set_book_style()
C = viz.COLORS
fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 5.6), gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [1.45, 1.0], "hspace": 0.42})

ink, soft, ok, bad = C["primary"], "#4A5568", C["GreenLine"], C["RedLine"]
rows = [
    ("proposer renewals", "task log + trigger line"),
    ("execution lease", "permission-path timer"),
    ("stop command", "logic analyzer"),
    ("drive frame", "fieldbus sniffer"),
    ("powered deceleration", "drive current + encoder"),
]
ys = [4, 3, 2, 1, 0]
H = 0.55
xmax = 130
for (name, witness), y in zip(rows, ys):
    ax.axhline(y, color=C["grid"], lw=0.6, zorder=1)

def step(y, t_on, hi_first, color, **kw):
    lo, hi = y, y + H
    if hi_first:
        xs, yy = [0, t_on, t_on, xmax], [hi, hi, lo, lo]
    else:
        xs, yy = [0, t_on, t_on, xmax], [lo, lo, hi, hi]
    ax.plot(xs, yy, color=color, lw=1.6, zorder=4, **kw)

# proposer: last valid renewal pulse at 0, task killed at 1 ms, probe refused at 65 ms
ax.plot([0, 0, 1.2, 1.2, xmax], [4, 4 + H, 4 + H, 4, 4], color=ink, lw=1.6, zorder=4)
ax.plot([1.2], [4 + H + 0.12], marker="x", color=bad, ms=6, mew=1.6, zorder=5)
ax.text(3.0, 4 + H + 0.12, "task killed", fontsize=7.5, color=bad, va="center")
ax.plot([t_probe, t_probe], [4, 4 + H * 0.7], color=soft, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=4)
ax.text(t_probe - 1.5, 4 + H * 0.45, f"probe proposal at {t_probe:.0f} ms, refused", fontsize=7.5, color=soft, va="center", ha="right")
# lease valid until expiry
step(3, t_lease, True, ink)
ax.text(t_lease + 1.5, 3 + H + 0.08, f"expires {t_lease:.0f} ms", fontsize=7.5, color=ink, va="bottom")
step(2, t_cmd, False, ink)
ax.text(t_cmd + 1.5, 2 + H + 0.08, f"next tick {t_cmd:.0f} ms", fontsize=7.5, color=ink, va="bottom")
step(1, t_frame, False, ink)
ax.text(t_frame + 1.5, 1 + H + 0.08, f"bus {t_frame:.0f} ms", fontsize=7.5, color=ink, va="bottom")
# onset allowance window and the two onsets
ax.fill_between([t_frame, t_onset], -0.15, H + 0.15, color=C["GreenL"], alpha=0.8, zorder=0, lw=0)
ax.text((t_frame + t_onset) / 2, H + 0.2, "onset\nallowance", fontsize=7.0, color=ok, ha="center", va="bottom")
ax.axvline(t_onset, color=ok, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=2)
ax.plot([0, t_onset, t_onset, xmax], [0, 0, H, H], color=ok, lw=1.8, zorder=5, label="onset at the bound")
ax.plot([0, t_late, t_late, xmax], [0, 0, H, H], color=bad, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=5, label="late-onset example")
ax.annotate("", xy=(t_late, -0.32), xytext=(t_onset, -0.32), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=bad, lw=1.0))
ax.text((t_onset + t_late) / 2, -0.42, f"onset margin $\\rho$ = \u2212{t_late - t_onset:.0f} ms", fontsize=7.5, color=bad, ha="center", va="top")
ax.text(t_onset - 1.5, 4.95, f"onset bound {t_onset:.0f} ms", fontsize=7.5, color=ok, ha="right", va="bottom")

ax.set_yticks([y + H / 2 for y in ys])
ax.set_yticklabels([f"{n}\n({w})" for n, w in rows], fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_xlim(-3, xmax)
ax.set_ylim(-0.95, 5.25)
ax.set_xticks(range(0, xmax + 1, 10))
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=8)
ax.set_xlabel("time after the last valid renewal (ms)", fontsize=9)
ax.grid(False)
for s in ("top", "right", "left"):
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0)

# speed panel
bx.axvspan(0, xmax, color=C["grid"], alpha=0.25, lw=0, zorder=0)
bx.text(xmax / 2, 0.08, f"0 to {xmax} ms,\npanel above", fontsize=7.0, color=soft, ha="center", va="bottom")
bx.plot(t, v_bound, color=ok, lw=1.8, zorder=4)
bx.plot(t, v_late, color=bad, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=4)
end_b = t_onset + T_stop * 1000
end_l = t_late + T_stop * 1000
bx.text(
    end_b - 30,
    0.52,
    f"rest at {end_b:,.0f} ms\ntravel {R.f1_aisle_stop_bound.magnitude:.1f} mm\n(at the oracle bound)",
    fontsize=7.5,
    color=ok,
    ha="right",
    va="center",
)
bx.text(
    end_l + 25,
    0.36,
    f"rest at {end_l:,.0f} ms\ntravel {R.travel_late.magnitude:.1f} mm\n$\\rho$ = \u2212{-R.rho_dist.magnitude:.0f} mm",
    fontsize=7.5,
    color=bad,
    ha="left",

bx.set_xlim(-3, 1250)
bx.set_ylim(0, v0 * 1.18)
bx.set_xlabel("time after the last valid renewal (ms)", fontsize=9)
bx.set_ylabel("base speed (m/s)", fontsize=9)
bx.tick_params(labelsize=8)
bx.text(8, v0 + 0.05, f"{v0:.1f} m/s aisle speed", fontsize=7.5, color=ink, va="bottom")
for s in ("top", "right"):
    bx.spines[s].set_visible(False)
```
