
:::

@Fig-15-hardware-fault-injection draws this trace against its oracle, channel by channel. Each channel comes from a different instrument, so a trial that fails can show where it failed: a lease that expired on time and a stop command issued on the next tick, followed by a late onset, place the fault in the fieldbus or the drive rather than in the permission path.

Robustness transforms verification into **temporal logic falsification as adversarial optimization**\index{Temporal logic falsification!definition}. In classical machine learning, adversarial attacks such as the fast gradient sign method (FGSM) [@goodfellow2015explaining] and projected gradient descent (PGD) [@madry2018towards] search for an input perturbation $\delta$ within an $\epsilon$-ball ($\|\delta\|_\infty \le \epsilon$) that maximizes task loss: $\max_{\|\delta\|_\infty \le \epsilon} \mathcal{L}(f(x + \delta), y)$. In cyber-physical verification, temporal logic falsification is the continuous dynamic equivalent: rather than perturbing static feature vectors, an adversarial optimizer searches over initial condition spaces and time-varying physical disturbance trajectories within a bounded physical disturbance budget to minimize quantitative STL robustness. The robustness score acts directly as the adversarial falsification loss.

Uniform random sampling of a high-dimensional state space requires an intractable number of trials to observe a rare corner-case collision; an adversarial falsification engine searches actively for the disturbance sequences that drive the system closest to invariant violation.

### Formulating falsification as trajectory optimization {#sec-verification-falsification-trajectory-formulation}

Formally, let $\theta_0 \in \Theta_0$ represent the machine's initial state vector (speed, payload, heading, battery state-of-charge), and let $w(t) \in \mathcal{W}$ denote an adversarial disturbance trajectory spanning the test horizon $[0, T]$. In physical systems, $w(t)$ cannot be an unconstrained discontinuous function: physical actuators, sensors, and environmental states have finite bandwidth and inertia. We therefore parameterize disturbance trajectories over a compact parameter space $\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{P}$ using smooth basis functions (such as B-splines, cubic splines, or Fourier series):
$$w(t; \mathbf{p}) = \sum_{k=1}^K \mathbf{p}_k B_k(t)$$
where $B_k(t)$ are time-dependent basis functions and $\mathbf{p}_k$ are bounded coefficients.

The temporal logic falsification problem is formulated as finding the worst-case parameter combination that minimizes quantitative robustness:
$$\min_{\theta_0 \in \Theta_0, \, \mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{P}} \rho(\phi, s(\theta_0, w(\mathbf{p})), 0) \quad \text{subject to} \quad \|w(t; \mathbf{p})\|_\infty \le \Delta_w, \quad \forall t \in [0, T].$$ {#eq-verification-adversarial-falsification}

The disturbance budget $\Delta_w$ in @eq-verification-adversarial-falsification constrains the magnitude of the optical, acoustic, contact, and execution disturbances already derived from the envelope. Magnitude alone does not make a trajectory realizable. The basis, coefficient bounds, and test fixture must also represent its rate of change and duration. A programmable load that cannot reproduce a simulated voltage transient leaves that counterexample untested on hardware.

The campaign therefore retains both the requested disturbance and its independently measured realization. If the fixture fails to deliver the precommitted disturbance, the trial is invalid for that test even if the machine stops. A realizable counterexample can reject the stated claim; a successful search over a restricted parameterization still leaves disturbances outside that parameterization open.

### Selecting a search method {#sec-verification-optimization-engines}

Contact transitions and discrete controller states can make the robustness objective nonsmooth, so derivative-free methods are useful. Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES) [@hansen2001completely] adapts a distribution over disturbance parameters and can explore correlated changes in speed, friction, and timing. Bayesian optimization[^fn-bayesian-optimization-surrogate] uses a surrogate and its uncertainty to select additional trials when physical runs are expensive. Neither method guarantees a global minimum from a finite campaign. The record retains search bounds, seeds, evaluated cases, and fixture constraints so that another engineer can identify what was actually challenged.

[^fn-bayesian-optimization-surrogate]: **Bayesian Optimization**\index{Bayesian optimization!expensive trials}: The method came from engineering design, where each evaluation was a costly simulation. @jones1998efficient fitted a Gaussian-process surrogate to the runs made so far and chose the next run where its expected improvement was largest. A physical fault rig has the same economics, since each trial costs a reset, an inspection, and a cool-down. The surrogate's confidence is still a model's, however, and a region it predicts to be safe has not been tested until a run lands there.

Two established toolboxes package this loop for models of cyber-physical systems. S-TaLiRo [@annpureddy2011staliro] and Breach [@donze2010breach] take an STL requirement and a simulation model, compute robustness on each simulated trace, and drive a stochastic or local optimizer toward negative robustness. A related family treats the disturbance sequence itself as the decision variable. **Adaptive stress testing**\index{Adaptive stress testing} [@lee2020adaptive] searches the disturbance sequence with Monte Carlo tree search or reinforcement learning for the most likely path to failure, not merely any path, which ranks counterexamples by how plausible their disturbances are. A survey of these black-box methods organizes them by what each returns: a counterexample, the most likely failure, or a failure probability [@corso2021survey]. Only the last of these is an estimate of operational risk, and @sec-verification-importance-sampling shows what it takes.

::: {#chk-verification-temporal-logic-oracles-and-falsification .callout-checkpoint title="Temporal logic oracles and test precommitment"}

Before executing automated falsification against physical AI policies, verify your understanding of temporal logic specifications and test validity criteria:

- [ ] **Quantitative robustness interpretation**: Can you explain how Signal Temporal Logic replaces binary pass/fail assertions with a signed predicate margin, and how its units and reference limit determine the meaning of a negative score?
- [ ] **Adversarial optimization of disturbance trajectories**: Can you describe how black-box optimizers use quantitative robustness scores to discover worst-case combinations of latency, noise, and friction?
- [ ] **Test invalidation vs. failure criteria**: Can you distinguish between an execution that falsifies a safety invariant and an invalid trial where testbed preconditions or fault injection mechanisms failed?
- [ ] **Normalization scale estimate**: For the late F1 trace of @sec-verification-stl-robustness, suppose the record had fixed the distance scale at the `{python} RackEndVerification.eps_track_str` tracking inset while keeping the `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str` onset scale. Can you estimate both normalized margins and say which predicate would then set the combined score?

:::

Search returns candidate counterexamples and measured margins. When a candidate comes from simulation, using it in a physical claim requires an account of the discrepancy between the modeled and actual trajectories.

### Sim-to-real transfer validation and discrepancy bounds {#sec-verification-sim-to-real-bounds}

In physical AI systems, high-throughput software-in-the-loop simulation is indispensable for exploring combinatorial corner cases, but relying on simulation assertions without bounding transfer error is the digital twin delusion in its plainest form, because an unvalidated simulator can only confirm what its model already assumes. To use simulation sweeps as valid evidentiary warrants in a structured safety case, the engineering team must formally validate and bound the **sim-to-real transfer gap** $\epsilon_{\text{gap}}$\index{Sim-to-real transfer gap!discrepancy bounds}\index{Simulation-to-reality leap!validation bounds}.

Let $s_{\text{sim}}(t; \theta, u) \in \mathcal{S}$ and $s_{\text{real}}(t; \theta, u) \in \mathcal{S}$ denote the system state trajectories in simulation and on target physical hardware under matched declared conditions $\theta$ (initial speed, payload, floor friction) and input history $u$. Replaying identical inputs establishes an open-loop comparison. A claim about the deployed policy instead requires a discrepancy bound for matched closed-loop trials, including the different commands that changed observations can induce; the input-replay bound alone cannot establish it. The continuous transfer discrepancy is the supremum error across the test horizon $[0, T]$ measured under a task-weighted physical norm:
$$\epsilon_{\text{gap}} = \sup_{t \in [0, T]} \|s_{\text{real}}(t) - s_{\text{sim}}(t)\|_W$$ {#eq-verification-sim2real-gap}
where $\|\cdot\|_W$ first divides position, velocity, and actuator torque errors by predeclared positive reference scales in meters, meters per second, and newton-meters, respectively, then applies dimensionless task weights. The record fixes those scales and weights; the resulting discrepancy is dimensionless, and $L_\phi$ has the units of the predicate margin.

The transfer calculation requires a bound that applies to the claimed trajectories, rather than only the largest discrepancy observed in a finite test. In plain terms, the allowable model error must be subtracted from the simulated margin. Consider an STL safety requirement $\phi$ whose atomic predicates $f(s(t)) \ge 0$ are Lipschitz continuous with Lipschitz constant $L_\phi = \sup_{s_1 \ne s_2} |f(s_1) - f(s_2)| / \|s_1 - s_2\|_W$. In plain terms, $L_\phi$ is the largest rate at which the margin can change per unit of state error; for a clearance predicate in meters and a norm that measures position error in meters, it is 1. By Lipschitz continuity, the physical predicate error is bounded pointwise by the state discrepancy:
$$|f(s_{\text{real}}(t)) - f(s_{\text{sim}}(t))| \le L_\phi \|s_{\text{real}}(t) - s_{\text{sim}}(t)\|_W \le L_\phi \epsilon_{\text{gap}}$$
which guarantees that at every instant $t \in [0, T]$:
$$f(s_{\text{real}}(t)) \ge f(s_{\text{sim}}(t)) - L_\phi \epsilon_{\text{gap}}.$$
Taking the infimum across the temporal horizon $t \in [0, T]$ for an invariance property $\phi \equiv \square_{[0, T]} (f(s(t)) \ge 0)$, the guaranteed lower bound on physical robustness in the real world is:
$$\rho_{\text{real}} \ge \rho_{\text{sim}} - L_\phi \epsilon_{\text{gap}}.$$ {#eq-verification-robustness-discount}
The term $L_\phi \epsilon_{\text{gap}}$ in @eq-verification-robustness-discount acts as a **sim-to-real robustness discount**. If simulated robustness $\rho_{\text{sim}}$ is smaller than $L_\phi \epsilon_{\text{gap}}$, the simulation pass guarantees no physical margin at all: the real system can breach the safe invariant set ($\rho_{\text{real}} < 0$) even though every simulated trial returned a positive margin.

The rack-end claim makes the discount concrete. Score the distance predicate in meters and let the norm measure position error with a 1 m scale, a modeling choice that makes $L_\phi = 1$. Suppose a simulated stop ends with the whole `{python} RackEndVerification.spare_str` reserve intact. The discount of @eq-verification-robustness-discount then leaves a positive physical margin only if $\epsilon_{\text{gap}} <$ `{python} RackEndVerification.eps_gap_max_str`, that is, only if the simulated and real trajectories never differ by as much as the reserve itself. A simulator whose stopping position is validated to within a few centimeters transfers most of the margin; one that has never been compared with a measured stop transfers none of it.

The coupled-boundary examples identify what this discount must cover: drivetrain lag changes delivered torque, contact conditions change braking traction, and target execution changes response time. A bound calibrated with an unloaded, cool machine cannot silently extend to a loaded, thermally throttled one. The record must state the conditions over which the discrepancy bound is justified and separate that bound from the largest error merely observed in the paired trials.

The measurement behind $\hat{\epsilon}_{\text{gap}}$ is the paired probing that already qualifies the simulator for training (@sec-training-contact-exploit), which drives identical commands into the simulated and physical plant and scores each channel of the gap against its tolerance (@sec-training-sim-to-real-gap). Verification reuses that procedure with two changes. The excitations are chosen by the claim under test, braking from aisle speed for the rack-end claim rather than latch approaches, and the physical trajectories are measured by instrumentation independent of the machine's own sensors, so that a shared sensor error cannot cancel out of the difference. The resulting $\hat{\epsilon}_{\text{gap}}$ is recorded with the fault records, together with the conditions over which it was measured. If the transfer argument relies on domain randomization distributions $\mathcal{D}_{\text{DR}}$ covering physical hardware dispersion, it must justify the following inclusion over the claimed conditions; finite paired measurements can challenge the inclusion but cannot establish it globally:
$$\mathcal{S}_{\text{real}}(\theta) \subseteq \bigcup_{\tilde{\theta} \sim \mathcal{D}_{\text{DR}}} \mathcal{S}_{\text{sim}}(\tilde{\theta}).$$
If unmodeled physical effects, such as actuator latency, stator saturation, gear backlash, or Coulomb stiction, cause physical trajectories to escape the randomized simulation bundle, the sim-to-real transfer is unvalidated, and software-in-the-loop test passes cannot serve as warrants in the release safety case.
## Interpreting Campaign Statistics {#sec-verification-campaign-statistics}

A list of adversarial trials is not yet an estimate of operational risk. The sampling procedure determines which population a statistic describes, and missing witnesses remain missing evidence in every analysis.

```{python}
#| label: calc-verify-injected-population-trials
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ZERO-MISS INJECTION COUNTS FOR A SAMPLED FAULT POPULATION (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: fault-manifest section and @nbk-verification-hardware-fault-injection-coverage-mean-time.
# │ Show: Zero-miss injections needed to put a one-sided upper limit on the miss probability,
# │       and the coverage (98.98 and 99.90 percent) and injection counts (293 and 2,935)
# │       that the notebook's illustrative FIT rates and chosen targets imply.
# │ How: n = ceil(ln(1 - C) / ln(1 - p)), the zero-failure sizing of @sec-evaluation-trial-limits.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_zero_failure_sample_size
import math
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_percent, fmt_int, fmt_display_math, check

class InjectedPopulationTrials:
    """Zero-miss injection counts for a declared fault population."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    confidence = 0.95  # category: chosen
    # Component fault rates for the coverage notebook, in FIT (faults per 1e9 h)
    fit_sensors = 1500  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    fit_compute = 1000  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    fit_power = 2500  # transceivers and power management; scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    fit_gate = 4800  # gate drivers; scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    fit_target_1 = 100  # unmitigated-rate target; category: chosen
    fit_target_2 = 10  # tighter unmitigated-rate target; category: chosen

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    fit_raw = fit_sensors + fit_compute + fit_power + fit_gate
    c_diag_1 = 1.0 - fit_target_1 / fit_raw  # required coverage: lambda_raw (1 - C) <= target
    c_diag_2 = 1.0 - fit_target_2 / fit_raw
    # Injections that demonstrate each coverage: miss probability p = 1 - C_diag
    n_cov_1 = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(c_diag_1, confidence=confidence)
    n_cov_2 = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(c_diag_2, confidence=confidence)
    n_cov_1_exact = math.log(1.0 - confidence) / math.log(c_diag_1)
    rule3_1 = 3.0 * fit_raw / fit_target_1  # the rule-of-three approximation 3/p
    rule3_2 = 3.0 * fit_raw / fit_target_2

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(fit_raw == 9800, "Component fault rates must sum to 9,800 FIT")
    check(c_diag_1 < c_diag_2 < 1.0, "A tighter target must need more coverage")
    check(n_cov_1 == 293 and n_cov_2 == 2935, "Coverage counts drifted from 293 and 2,935.")
    check(abs(n_cov_1 - rule3_1) < 2 and abs(n_cov_2 - rule3_2) < 6, "The counts sit within a few injections of 3/p.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    confidence_pct_str = fmt_percent(confidence, precision=0)
    fit_sensors_str = fmt_int(fit_sensors, commas=True)
    fit_compute_str = fmt_int(fit_compute, commas=True)
    fit_power_str = fmt_int(fit_power, commas=True)
    fit_gate_str = fmt_int(fit_gate, commas=True)
    fit_target_1_str = fmt_int(fit_target_1)
    fit_target_2_str = fmt_int(fit_target_2)
    c_diag_1_pct2_str = fmt_percent(c_diag_1, precision=2)
    c_diag_2_pct2_str = fmt_percent(c_diag_2, precision=2)
    n_cov_1_str = fmt_int(n_cov_1, commas=True)
    n_cov_2_str = fmt_int(n_cov_2, commas=True)
    rule3_2_str = fmt_int(round(rule3_2), commas=True)
    raw_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\lambda_{{\text{{raw}}}} = {fit_sensors} + {fit_compute} + {fit_power} + {fit_gate} = {fit_raw}\ \text{{FIT}}, \qquad"
        rf" C_{{\text{{diag}}}} \ge 1 - \frac{{\lambda_{{\text{{target}}}}}}{{\lambda_{{\text{{raw}}}}}} = 1 - \frac{{{fit_target_1}}}{{{fit_raw}}} = {fmt(c_diag_1, precision=4)}"
    )
    count_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"n \ge \frac{{\ln(1 - C)}}{{\ln C_{{\text{{diag}}}}}} = \frac{{\ln {fmt(1.0 - confidence, precision=2)}}}{{\ln {fmt(c_diag_1, precision=4)}}}"
        rf" = {fmt(n_cov_1_exact, precision=1)} \;\Rightarrow\; n = {n_cov_1}, \qquad \frac{{3}}{{p}} = \frac{{3 \lambda_{{\text{{raw}}}}}}{{\lambda_{{\text{{target}}}}}} = \frac{{3 \times {fit_raw}}}{{{fit_target_1}}} = {round(rule3_1)}"
    )
```

When $n$ independent Bernoulli trials sampled from the declared fault distribution have zero missed mitigations, the result sets a one-sided upper confidence limit on the miss probability for that distribution. The count is the zero-failure sizing of @sec-evaluation-trial-limits, applied to an injected fault population rather than to runs of a policy. It bounds the miss probability at $p$ with confidence $C$ once $(1-p)^n \le 1 - C$, which at `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.confidence_pct_str` percent takes roughly $3/p$ zero-miss injections. To infer a FIT-weighted hardware coverage (\ref{nbk-verification-hardware-fault-injection-coverage-mean-time} defines the FIT rate and the weights $\lambda_i$), injections must represent the raw-fault weights $\lambda_i$ or use a justified stratified weighting and per-stratum analysis.[^fn-math-zero-failure]

[^fn-math-zero-failure]: **Trial sampling and aging**\index{Zero-failure testing!independence}: The binomial count assumes independent, identically distributed Bernoulli outcomes under the declared injection distribution; it does not require Poisson event arrivals. Repeated heating, wear, or contact changes can break independence and require a state-stratified test design.

The bound applies only when the injection outcomes meet the declared independence and sampling assumptions. Repeated stops heat the drive windings ($I^2R$)\index{Joule heating!fault coupling} and the brake lining, change their resistance and friction, and couple later trials to earlier ones. A campaign run on a dry aisle at room temperature cannot establish a limit for an inspected floor or for the envelope's `{python} RackEndVerification.ambient_lo_str` end.

::: {#nbk-verification-hardware-fault-injection-coverage-mean-time .callout-notebook title="The coverage count"}

**Problem**: Illustrative component fault rates and a chosen ceiling on the unmitigated rate fix the diagnostic coverage the machine needs. How many zero-miss injections, sampled in proportion to those rates, would demonstrate that coverage?

**Variables**:

* Component fault rates $\lambda_i$ in FIT, one fault per $10^9$ operating hours (Illustrative): sensors `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.fit_sensors_str`, compute `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.fit_compute_str`, transceivers and power management `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.fit_power_str`, and gate drivers `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.fit_gate_str`.
* Target unmitigated rate $\lambda_{\text{target}} =$ `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.fit_target_1_str` FIT, with a stricter `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.fit_target_2_str` FIT alternative, at confidence $C =$ `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.confidence_pct_str` percent (Chosen).
* Diagnostic coverage $C_{\text{diag}}$, the $\lambda_i$-weighted fraction of faults whose hazardous effect is mitigated, so that $\lambda_{\text{unmitigated}} = \lambda_{\text{raw}}(1 - C_{\text{diag}})$ and a single injection misses with probability $p = 1 - C_{\text{diag}}$.

**Math**:

*Required coverage.*
`{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.raw_math`

*Injections to demonstrate it*, from the zero-failure count of @sec-evaluation-trial-limits.
`{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.count_math`

*Sensitivity.* The count scales as $3\lambda_{\text{raw}}/\lambda_{\text{target}}$, so the `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.fit_target_2_str` FIT target needs `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.c_diag_2_pct2_str` percent coverage and `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.n_cov_2_str` injections, against a rule-of-three estimate of `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.rule3_2_str`.

**Result**: A `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.fit_target_1_str` FIT target needs `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.c_diag_1_pct2_str` percent coverage, which `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.n_cov_1_str` zero-miss injections demonstrate at `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.confidence_pct_str` percent confidence.

**Systems insight**: The rate target, not the length of the fault list, sets the size of the campaign, and every tenfold tightening costs ten times the injections. The count holds only for injections drawn in proportion to $\lambda_i$. Uniform injections across unequal-rate components estimate a different distribution unless outcomes are weighted and each stratum has adequate evidence, and each injection must record which mode was injected, whether it was detected, and whether the plant reached its allowed state.

:::

Operating hours cannot close what the injections leave open. A zero-event test cannot reach the hazard rates a release claim needs (the exposure wall of @sec-evaluation-trial-limits), so the fault record carries what was never injected as prominently as what passed. It lists every parameter combination omitted because of bench limits, sensor bandwidth, or destructive-test cost, and an untested region therefore cannot reach the safety case of @sec-release as a verified margin.

### Exposure and the population a statistic describes {#sec-verification-exposure-wall}

Operational exposure and deliberate fault injection sample different populations. Under a constant-rate Poisson model, zero occurrences of a specified event over $N$ hours gives the following exposure requirement for a one-sided confidence level $C$:
$$-\lambda N \le \ln(1 - C) \implies N \ge \frac{-\ln(1 - C)}{\lambda}.$$

At 95 percent confidence $-\ln(1-C) \approx 3$, which is the time-domain form of the rule of three that @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-survival derives for trials (@eq-eval-rule-of-three); that section owns the zero-failure bound, and the exposure form here only restates it in operating hours. The inverse dependence on the target event rate is the exposure limitation analyzed by @butler1993infeasibility. More fleet hours do not test an omitted fault or establish standards compliance. The event definition, operating conditions, intervention policy, and configuration must match before exposure can support the bound; a changed policy or driver requires an argument for reusing earlier exposure.

### Estimating a rare failure rate by importance sampling {#sec-verification-importance-sampling}

Falsification answers whether a failure exists. Release often needs a different number: how often the failure occurs under the conditions the machine will actually meet. Plain Monte Carlo sampling from those conditions wastes almost every run on a comfortable stop, and a zero-failure campaign bounds the rate only at the scale @sec-evaluation-trial-limits derives. **Importance sampling**\index{Importance sampling!definition}[^fn-importance-sampling-shielding] draws the runs from a different distribution that visits the failure region often, then weights each run to undo the bias.

[^fn-importance-sampling-shielding]: **Importance Sampling**\index{Importance sampling!origins}: The method grew out of Monte Carlo calculations of radiation shielding in the early 1950s, in which the particles that mattered, the few that penetrated the shield, were as rare as overshooting stops are here. @kahn1953methods set it out, beside correlated sampling and statistical estimation, as a general way to cut the runs an estimate needs. The danger arrived with the method. A proposal that never visits a penetration path reports a small variance and a confident, wrong answer, which is the support failure the diagnostics below must rule out.

```{python}
#| label: calc-verify-rare-event-is
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ IMPORTANCE SAMPLING AND THE CROSS-ENTROPY METHOD ON THE RACK-END OVERSHOOT (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-verification-importance-sampling.
# │ Goal: Estimate the probability that an unbudgeted queue delay exhausts the
# │       rack-end reserve, and compare plain Monte Carlo, zero-failure testing,
# │       and importance sampling with a cross-entropy proposal.
# │ Show: failure when the delay exceeds T_latest = 100.8 ms; with an
# │       exponential delay of mean 5 ms, p = 1.8e-9; plain Monte Carlo needs
# │       5.7e10 runs for 10 percent relative error, zero-failure testing 1.7e9;
# │       the cross-entropy proposal (mean 105.8 ms after 4 levels) needs about
# │       2,700 runs, within 0.1 percent of the best exponential proposal.
# │ How: closed forms for an exponential operational delay and an exponential
# │      proposal; the expected (large-sample) cross-entropy iteration
# │      (calc_monte_carlo_sample_size, calc_importance_sampling_exponential,
# │      calc_cross_entropy_exponential_proposal,
# │      calc_optimal_exponential_proposal_mean).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_zero_failure_sample_size
from mlsysim.physics import (
    calc_monte_carlo_sample_size,
    calc_importance_sampling_exponential,
    calc_cross_entropy_exponential_proposal,
    calc_optimal_exponential_proposal_mean,
)
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_sci, fmt_latency, fmt_percent, check

class RareEventOvershoot:
    """Likelihood-ratio estimate of the rack-end reserve-exhaustion probability."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_exhaust = RackEndVerification.t_spare  # queue delay that spends the reserve (T_latest); category: derived
    d_mean = (
        5 * millisecond
    )  # mean unbudgeted queue delay per stop, exponential; scenario assumption; category: illustrative (a loaded-trial delay histogram would replace it)
    elite_share = 0.1  # cross-entropy elite fraction; category: chosen
    rel_err = 0.1  # target relative standard error of the estimate; category: chosen
    confidence = 0.95  # category: chosen

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    gamma = float(t_exhaust.to(millisecond).magnitude)
    m0 = float(d_mean.to(millisecond).magnitude)
    # Cross-entropy iteration (expected, large-sample form): raise the level to the
    # (1 - elite_share) quantile of the current proposal, refit the proposal mean
    # to the likelihood-weighted elite samples, which for this family is the
    # conditional mean E_p[D | D > level] = level + m0.
    ce = calc_cross_entropy_exponential_proposal(t_exhaust, d_mean, elite_share)
    levels = [lv.to(millisecond).magnitude for lv in ce["levels"]]
    n_levels = ce["n_levels"]
    m_ce = ce["proposal_mean"].to(millisecond).magnitude
    is_ce = calc_importance_sampling_exponential(t_exhaust, d_mean, ce["proposal_mean"])
    p_true = is_ce["failure_probability"]  # P(D > T_latest) under the operational model
    n_mc = calc_monte_carlo_sample_size(p_true, rel_err)  # plain Monte Carlo runs for the target error
    n_zero = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(1.0 - p_true, confidence=confidence)  # @sec-evaluation-trial-limits
    relvar_ce = is_ce["relative_variance"]  # per-sample relative variance
    n_is = relvar_ce / rel_err**2
    p_q_fail = is_ce["proposal_failure_share"]  # share of proposal draws that land in the failure set
    ess_per_draw = is_ce["ess_per_draw"]  # expected (sum w)^2 / sum w^2 per draw
    n_ess = n_is * ess_per_draw
    # Best exponential proposal (minimum second moment)
    m_opt = calc_optimal_exponential_proposal_mean(t_exhaust, d_mean)
    relvar_opt = calc_importance_sampling_exponential(t_exhaust, d_mean, m_opt)["relative_variance"]
    ce_penalty = relvar_ce / relvar_opt - 1.0
    speedup = n_mc / n_is

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(gamma - 100.775) < 5e-3, "Failure threshold is the 100.8 ms spare-exhaustion delay.")
    check(1e-9 < p_true < 1e-8, "Operational failure probability is of order 1e-9.")
    check(n_levels == 4 and abs(m_ce - (gamma + m0)) < 1e-9, "Cross-entropy reaches the threshold in four levels.")
    check(0 <= ce_penalty < 1e-3, "The cross-entropy proposal is within 0.1 percent of the best exponential proposal.")
    check(n_is < 1e4 < n_zero < n_mc, "Importance sampling needs orders of magnitude fewer runs.")
    check(0.3 < p_q_fail < 0.5, "Roughly two in five proposal draws land in the failure set.")
    # margin_rare_event_runs_ladder.svg fig-alt hand-types 5.7e10, 1.7e9, and 2,709 runs
    check(
        f"{n_mc:.1e}" == "5.7e+10" and f"{n_zero:.1e}" == "1.7e+09" and math.ceil(n_is) == 2709,
        "Runs-ladder fig-alt: 5.7e10, 1.7e9, 2,709.",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    d_mean_str = fmt_latency(d_mean, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    p_true_str = fmt_sci(p_true, precision=1)
    n_mc_str = fmt_sci(n_mc, precision=1)
    n_zero_str = fmt_sci(n_zero, precision=1)
    elite_pct_str = fmt_percent(elite_share, precision=0, style="prose")
    rel_err_pct_str = fmt_percent(rel_err, precision=0, style="prose")
    level_1_str = fmt_latency(levels[0] * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    level_2_str = fmt_latency(levels[1] * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    level_3_str = fmt_latency(levels[2] * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    n_levels_str = fmt_int(n_levels)
    m_ce_str = fmt_latency(m_ce * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    p_q_fail_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_q_fail, precision=1, style="prose")
    relvar_ce_str = fmt(relvar_ce, precision=1)
    n_is_str = fmt_int(math.ceil(n_is), commas=True)
    n_ess_str = fmt_int(round(n_ess), commas=True)
    speedup_str = fmt_sci(speedup, precision=0)
```

Write the operational distribution of the uncertain inputs $x$ as $p(x)$ and the failure event as $F$. Plain Monte Carlo estimates $P_F = \Pr_p(x \in F)$ as the fraction of $N$ draws from $p$ that fail. Importance sampling draws instead from a **proposal distribution** $q(x)$ and weights each draw by the **likelihood ratio** $w(x) = p(x)/q(x)$:
$$\hat{P}_F = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbb{1}[x_i \in F]\, w(x_i), \qquad x_i \sim q.$$ {#eq-verification-importance-sampling}
The estimator is unbiased whenever $q$ is positive wherever $p$ assigns probability to failure, because the weight exactly undoes the change of distribution [@owen2013monte]. Its variance depends on the choice of $q$. The ideal proposal is $p$ restricted to $F$ and renormalized, which gives every draw the same weight $P_F$ and zero variance; it cannot be used, because building it requires the unknown $P_F$. Practical proposals approximate it.

The **cross-entropy method**\index{Cross-entropy method} [@rubinstein2004cross] finds such an approximation within a chosen family $q_\theta$ by working up through a sequence of easier events. Starting from $q_{\theta_0} = p$, each iteration draws a batch from the current proposal, sets an intermediate level at the $(1-\beta)$ quantile of the failure measure so that a fraction $\beta$ of the batch clears it, and refits $\theta$ by maximizing the likelihood-weighted log-density of those elite draws. The level rises each round until it reaches the true failure threshold, and the final proposal concentrates where failures are most probable under $p$. For an exponential family the refit has a closed form: the new mean is the weighted mean of the elite draws.

Work it on the rack end. At the aisle speed the base covers the `{python} RackEndVerification.spare_str` reserve of @sec-verification-operating-envelope in $T_{\text{latest}} =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.t_spare_str`, so an unbudgeted queue of that length spends the whole reserve, and a stop overshoots the reserve when its queue delay $D$ exceeds that value. Take, as an illustrative operational model, an exponential delay with mean `{python} RareEventOvershoot.d_mean_str`, the tail of the simplest single-server queue model; a histogram of queue delays from loaded trials on the machine would replace it. Then $P_F = e^{-T_{\text{latest}}/\bar{D}} =$ `{python} RareEventOvershoot.p_true_str` per stop. That value is not a property of the machine; it is a value this simple model lets us compute exactly and use to check each estimator.

Every run count below follows from one fact about averages. If each of $N$ independent draws contributes a value with mean $P_F$ and variance $\sigma^2$, their average has standard deviation $\sigma/\sqrt{N}$, so its relative standard error is $r = \sqrt{\sigma^2/(P_F^2 N)}$ and the runs needed are $N = (\sigma^2/P_F^2)/r^2$. The ratio $\sigma^2/P_F^2$ is the per-draw **relative variance**. A plain Monte Carlo draw is a pass-or-fail indicator with variance $P_F(1-P_F)$, so plain Monte Carlo needs about $(1-P_F)/(P_F\,r^2)$ runs. Under the illustrative delay model, for $r$ of `{python} RareEventOvershoot.rel_err_pct_str` that is `{python} RareEventOvershoot.n_mc_str` stops. A zero-failure campaign needs `{python} RareEventOvershoot.n_zero_str` failure-free stops merely to bound the rate at $P_F$ (@eq-eval-rule-of-three).

The cross-entropy method with exponential proposals and an elite fraction of `{python} RareEventOvershoot.elite_pct_str` shows its mechanism plainly on this model. The first level is the 90th percentile of the operational delay, $\bar{D}\ln 10$, or `{python} RareEventOvershoot.level_1_str`. An exponential delay is memoryless: given that a delay already exceeds a level, its excess over that level is again exponential with mean $\bar{D}$. The weighted mean of the elite draws is therefore the level plus $\bar{D}$, and that becomes the next proposal mean. Repeating the step raises the level to `{python} RareEventOvershoot.level_2_str` and then `{python} RareEventOvershoot.level_3_str`, and at level `{python} RareEventOvershoot.n_levels_str` the percentile passes the threshold, so the level stops at $T_{\text{latest}}$ with a proposal mean of `{python} RareEventOvershoot.m_ce_str`, which is the operational model's mean delay given that the stop fails. Under that proposal `{python} RareEventOvershoot.p_q_fail_pct_str` of draws fail, and their small weights scale each failing draw's contribution back to the operational rate. The per-draw relative variance of the weighted indicator is `{python} RareEventOvershoot.relvar_ce_str`, so `{python} RareEventOvershoot.n_is_str` weighted draws reach the same `{python} RareEventOvershoot.rel_err_pct_str` error, about `{python} RareEventOvershoot.speedup_str` times fewer than plain Monte Carlo needs, and within a tenth of a percent of the best exponential proposal. Every one of these counts inherits the illustrative delay distribution; a measured delay histogram would change all of them.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_rare_event_runs_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Log-scale ladder of the runs needed to estimate one rare overshoot rate: 5.7 times 10 to the 10 for plain Monte Carlo, 1.7 times 10 to the 9 for a zero-failure campaign, and 2,709 for importance sampling with a cross-entropy proposal."}

*Weighting runs near failure cuts the runs by about `{python} RareEventOvershoot.speedup_str` times.*
:::

Two diagnostics keep the estimate honest. The **effective sample size**\index{Effective sample size}, $N_{\text{eff}} = \left(\sum_i w_i\right)^2 / \sum_i w_i^2$ [@owen2013monte], reports how many unweighted draws the weighted sample is worth; for the `{python} RareEventOvershoot.n_is_str` draws above its expected value is about `{python} RareEventOvershoot.n_ess_str`, and a value near 1 would mean a few heavy weights dominate. The second diagnostic is support. If the proposal's tail is lighter than $p$'s in some part of $F$, or misses a second failure mechanism altogether, the estimator can report a small variance while being badly wrong, and no statistic computed from the draws reveals the missing region. O'Kelly and colleagues applied the same adaptive importance sampling to end-to-end testing of an autonomous-driving stack and report substantial speedups over naive Monte Carlo evaluation of the same stack [@okelly2018scalable].

The contrast with falsification is now exact. A falsifier's search also concentrates runs near failure, but its sampling density is not written down, so its runs carry no weights, and the fraction of them that fail says nothing about $P_F$: in the illustrative example, roughly two in five proposal draws fail although the modeled operational rate is `{python} RareEventOvershoot.p_true_str`. An estimate reaches the fault records only with its declared $p$, its proposal $q$, the weights, the effective sample size, and the confidence interval, and it is a statement about the declared operational model, not a measurement of the machine.

### Extreme value theory and heavy-tailed safety distributions {#sec-verification-extreme-value-theory}

Importance sampling estimates the probability of one declared failure event. A release claim may also ask how large the worst overshoot is likely to be, and the telemetry supplies continuous margins to answer it: spatial clearance $d_{\text{clear}} - d(t)$, onset slack $t_{\text{bound}} - t_{\text{onset}}$, and torque headroom $\tau_{\text{max}} - \tau_{\text{act}}$. Near-misses carry information about the tail that a pass count discards.

Assuming a convenient tail model without establishing that it fits the measured quantity and sampling process is a common error\index{Extreme Value Theory!heavy tails}. A latency distribution with occasional contention bursts need not resemble the distribution measured on a quiet bus, and a Gaussian fitted to the bulk understates such a tail. Extreme value theory models rare extremes under stated assumptions; it does not establish that every physical AI system has a power-law tail or that a fitted endpoint is a hardware barrier.

**Extreme Value Theory (EVT)**\index{Extreme Value Theory!definition}\index{Generalized Pareto Distribution!GPD} supplies limiting families for extremes, much as the central limit theorem supplies one for sums [@coles2001introduction]. Its block-maxima form, the generalized extreme value distribution, is developed in @sec-appendix-ml-evt; the chapter uses the threshold form, which keeps every large observation rather than one maximum per block.

1. **Peaks over threshold and the Generalized Pareto Distribution**\index{Peaks-Over-Threshold!POT}\index{Generalized Pareto Distribution!Pickands-Balkema}: Model the exceedances $Y = X - u$ of a quantity $X$ over a sufficiently high threshold $u$. Under the Pickands-Balkema-de Haan theorem, which @balkema1974residual and @pickands1975statistical proved independently, the conditional distribution of those exceedances converges to the Generalized Pareto Distribution
$$H(y; \sigma_u, \xi) = 1 - \left( 1 + \frac{\xi y}{\sigma_u} \right)^{-1/\xi}, \quad y > 0,$$ {#eq-verification-gpd-distribution}
with scale $\sigma_u > 0$, support restricted to $1 + \xi y/\sigma_u > 0$, and the exponential limit at $\xi = 0$. The **shape parameter** $\xi$ sets the tail: $\xi > 0$ gives a heavy, power-law tail, $\xi = 0$ an exponential one, and $\xi < 0$ a bounded tail with finite endpoint $u - \sigma_u/\xi$.

2. **Return level**: For a return period[^fn-return-period-flood] $T$ expressed in the same sampling units as the exceedance rate, the **return level** $z_T$\index{Return level!EVT safety bounds} is the modeled level exceeded on average once every $T$ periods:
$$z_T = u + \frac{\sigma_u}{\xi} \left[ (T \zeta_u)^\xi - 1 \right]$$ {#eq-verification-evt-return-level}
where $\zeta_u = P(X > u) = N_u / N$ estimates the threshold exceedance probability per trial across $N$ trials, so $T$ is a number of such trials. The displayed form applies for $\xi \ne 0$; its continuous limit is $z_T = u + \sigma_u\ln(T\zeta_u)$ at $\xi = 0$. A return period in operating hours instead requires an exceedance rate per hour under the declared sampling and dependence model. The product $T\zeta_u$ must be dimensionless, and the calculation applies to return levels at or above $u$.

[^fn-return-period-flood]: **Return Period**\index{Return period!flood engineering}: The term comes from flood engineering, where the hundred-year flood is the level exceeded with probability one in a hundred in any year, and @gumbel1958statistics made return periods and return levels the working language of hydrology. The hydrologists' caution carries over intact. A return level extrapolates beyond the record, so it is only as honest as the threshold and the sampling behind it, and a return period counted in fault trials says nothing about operating hours until an exceedance rate per hour has been justified.

#### Connecting adversarial falsification to EVT tail sampling {#sec-verification-falsification-evt}

Under benign operation, exceedances of a conservative threshold are too rare to fit a tail; the exposure limit of @sec-verification-exposure-wall applies to them as much as to failures. Falsification concentrates runs near violation by optimizing over initial conditions $\theta_0 \in \Theta_0$ and disturbance coefficients $\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{P}$:
$$\min_{\theta_0 \in \Theta_0, \mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{P}} \rho\left(\phi, s(\theta_0, w(\mathbf{p})), 0\right).$$
For a stopping-distance overshoot $X = d_{\text{stop}} - d_{\text{budget}}$, that search deliberately fills the exceedance set
$$\mathcal{Y}_u = \{ Y_i = X_i - u \mid X_i > u \}$$
with observations, but under the search distribution, not the operational one. A tail fitted to those observations describes the search. It describes operation only if the runs came from a declared proposal and carry the likelihood-ratio weights of @eq-verification-importance-sampling, in which case the exceedance probability $\zeta_u$ and the fit use weighted counts.

A fitted shape is then a diagnostic, not a verdict on the architecture:

- **Positive shape ($\xi > 0$):** the model extrapolates a heavy upper tail. That does not prove that physical violations are unbounded or inevitable; the engineer must examine whether the fit, threshold, and sampling procedure support the proposed operating claim.
- **Negative shape ($\xi < 0$):** the model has a finite endpoint $u - \sigma_u/\xi$. That endpoint is not a measured hardware limit or proof that an enforcer always contains motion. The containment argument still depends on the enforcer's assumptions and the independent tests of its response.

#### Sim-to-real transfer bounds on EVT return levels {#sec-verification-evt-sim-to-real}

When high-throughput campaigns run on the software-in-the-loop and processor-in-the-loop (PIL) rungs of the qualification ladder, the fitted tail produces a simulated return level $z_{T, \text{sim}}$. As established in @sec-verification-sim-to-real-bounds, simulated and physical trajectories differ by a discrepancy $\epsilon_{\text{gap}} = \sup_t \|s_{\text{real}}(t) - s_{\text{sim}}(t)\|_W$. For a Lipschitz-continuous predicate with constant $L_\phi$, a justified bound on that discrepancy contributes the same additive discount as before (@eq-verification-evt-sim2real-bound):
$$z_{T, \text{real}} \le z_{T, \text{sim}} + L_\phi \epsilon_{\text{gap}}.$$ {#eq-verification-evt-sim2real-bound}
For the stated stopping claim, the discounted return level must fit inside the physical reserve:
$$z_{T, \text{sim}} + L_\phi \epsilon_{\text{gap}} \le d_{\text{clear}} - d_{\text{budget}}.$$ {#eq-verification-evt-release-condition}

The margin test in @eq-verification-evt-release-condition is a conditional check, not a sufficient release rule. It requires compatible simulation and physical populations, weighted samples if an operational return period is claimed, uncertainty in the fitted return level, and a discrepancy bound valid over the claimed conditions. A maximum discrepancy observed in a finite paired test does not by itself establish that bound.

For the rack-end claim, the reserve is `{python} RackEndVerification.spare_str`. A proposed tail estimate must state its population, weights, fit uncertainty, and transfer assumptions before it can be compared with that reserve. The F1 record has no measured trials, so it supplies neither a tail fit nor a return-level estimate. A fitted endpoint must never fill that missing-evidence field.

For the methods of this chapter's second half at full depth (falsification, failure-probability estimation, reachability, and runtime monitoring), the reference is *Algorithms for Validation* [@kochenderfer2026validation], whose algorithms operate on the same kind of declared system and property that a fault record carries.

Every statistic in this section is conditional. A zero-miss count describes the declared fault population, an exposure bound the configuration that accumulated the hours, an importance-sampling estimate its declared operational model, and a return level its fitted tail and transfer bound. Each of those conditions is a claim that can be wrong, so what the campaign hands on is not a single number but records that keep each measured margin beside the assumptions that license it.
## Fault Records for Release {#sec-verification-fault-manifest}

A completed F1 trial would join the renewal event, lease expiry, powered stop, and standstill on independent traces. No such measured trace is supplied here. Release can count that trial only if the trace stays bound to the claim, the envelope point, and the builds it tested. The fault record defined with the F1 trial links that header to the retained evidence bundle by cryptographic digest.

Release receives these claim-specific **fault records**\index{Fault record!release set} together with the coverage information needed to interpret them. The set binds the available fault records, qualification environments, justified transfer arguments, any applicable statistical estimates, and coverage deficits into an auditable ledger. Unmeasured or inapplicable fields remain explicit. The set supports the safety case of @sec-release-safety-cases-claims; its schema and signatures confer no authority beyond the evidence it contains.

Alongside the design contracts, the authority cases A1–A4, and the placement ledger that the fault list already draws on, the fault records consume two further sources: the omission log of the policy manifest (@sec-training-policy-manifest) and the coverage-gap catalog of the evaluation record (@sec-evaluation-logs), which name the operational conditions the learned proposer was never exposed to. Together, the header and bundle identify the claim, operating point, injection mechanism, hardware and software builds, raw trace, detector, response timing, physical outcome, and detected anomalies.

### The fault-record set specification {#sec-verification-contract-matrix}

Each record in the set exists to support one named claim of the release safety case, and its header states that claim. The F1 records support the claim that the permission path stops the loaded base within its travel bound after proposal renewal ceases; the F2 and F3 records support the same stopping claim when observations arrive stale or fieldbus frames are lost. The F4 records support the claim that the permission path, on its held-up rail, outlives a supply fault and completes the stop with every brake set. The actuator-jam record supports the claim that a blocked wheel is contained inside the side clearance without overheating its winding, the A1–A4 records support the claim that motion authority has one writer, cannot be bypassed, falls back when a handover stalls, and cannot be forged, and the proposer-injection record supports the claim that every proposal, however it was produced, meets the same permission checks. A record supports its claim only through an argument. For the rack-end claim, a brake-onset trace is evidence, and the argument must explain why its clock reference, injection, load, and floor conditions support the claimed response. How claims, arguments, and evidence compose into one reviewable case, and the notation that draws it, belong to release (@sec-release-assurance-grammar).

The records must also keep three failure domains apart, because each asks a different question about the same machine: faults of the safety-related control system (functional safety), hazards that arise with no fault at all from an insufficiency of the intended function, such as a perception or proposer blind spot (safety of the intended functionality, SOTIF\index{ISO 21448!SOTIF}), and deliberate attacks on sensors and channels (security). Which published document governs each part of the warehouse machine, at which edition, is the standards map of @sec-release-standards-map (@tbl-16-standards-map). A fault-injection pass does not by itself establish compliance or justify every operating condition. The release argument in @sec-release-safety-cases-claims evaluates which claims the assembled records support.

The individual fault records, qualification manifests, transfer gap bounds, and EVT tail parameters assemble into one signed set, the form in which the fault record, the thirteenth record in the record chain, reaches release\index{Fault record!schema specification}.

The signed set serves as the formal boundary between adversarial testing and operational release:

1. **Upstream Custody Lineage**:
   - Consumes the **authority record** (@sec-intervention-authority-log) to verify handover deadline timers ($T_{\text{timeout}}$, @sec-intervention-clearance-deadlines), duplicate-writer rejections (A1), and supervisory token integrity.
   - Consumes the **placement record** (@sec-placement-hardware-allocation) to verify bus contention limits, power-rail droop tolerances, and thermal dissipation thresholds.
   - Consumes the **enforcement record** and its admitted commands (@sec-enforcement-telemetry) to verify CBF invariant sets, QP filter execution deadlines, and fallback ladder transitions.
   - Consumes the **evaluation record** (@sec-evaluation-logs) to cross-reference offline covariate drift and simulation test catalogs against target hardware runs.
2. **Downstream Release Deliverables**:
   - Delivers to the **release manifest** and its safety case (@sec-release-safety-cases-claims) claim-specific evidence and its limits for the release argument.
   - Delivers to the **residual-claims register** (@sec-frontier-epistemic-limits) the explicit ledger of unverified envelope regimes, fixture bandwidth constraints, and epistemic boundaries.

@Tbl-15-verification-matrix-contract specifies the data schema of that set:

| Contract Field             | Type / Encoding             | Physical Semantic & Evidentiary Scope                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | Upstream Anchor / Derivation                                                                                                                                                    |
|:---------------------------|:----------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `matrix_id`                | `UUIDv5`                    | Stable namespace-and-name identifier for the campaign; not a digest of its completed results                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | Fixed at test orchestration initialization                                                                                                                                      |
| `matrix_digest`            | `SHA-256`                   | Digest of the canonical completed matrix payload, excluding digest and signature fields, binding manifest, build identity, calibration identities, and evidence references                                                                                                                                                                           | Computed after results are finalized; covered by the signed release record                                                                                                      |
| `qualification_manifest`   | `Struct<RungCoverage>`      | Executed run counts, throughputs, and fidelity mappings partitioned across the software-in-the-loop, PIL, HIL, and physical-rig rungs                                                                                                                                                                                                                | Four-stage qualification ladder (@sec-verification-qualification-rungs, @tbl-15-qualification-ladder)                                                                           |
| `fault_injection_ledger`   | `List<FaultRecordHeader>`   | Collection of cryptographically signed fault records across F1–F4, A1–A4, and compound cascades, partitioned into `PASS`, `FAIL`, `INVALID`, and `UNOBSERVABLE` verdicts                                                                                                                                                                             | Fault classification (@tbl-15-fault-classification) and static fault record (@tbl-15-f1-record)                                                                                 |
